articles.title: Vimeo to be acquired by Bending Spoons for $1.38 billion
articles.summary: The European software company Bending Spoons is acquiring the video hosting platform Vimeo for $1.38 billion. The deal is expected to close later this year.
articles.body: Vimeo is getting bought up by Bending Spoons, a European software company that has amassed a growing portfolio of businesses, including Evernote, WeTransfer, and Meetup. Bending Spoons will pay $1.38 billion to acquire the video hosting platform, and it expects to close the deal later this year. Vimeo launched in 2004 as a spinoff of CollegeHumor and has long struggled to keep up with its biggest rival: YouTube. In recent years, Vimeo has hiked video hosting fees and shifted toward catering to enterprise businesses as well as creators who want to monetize their content. Philip Moyer joined Vimeo as CEO last year as the company began dipping into AI tools. Just last week, Moyer announced that the platform is laying off around 10 percent of the company’s workforce. Bending Spoon’s deal to acquire Vimeo will take the video hosting platform private. Over the years, Bending Spoons hasn’t garnered the best reputation, as it has issued layoffs across many of the companies it acquired and introduced new limitations on Evernote’s free plan, while also raising the price of TapeACall’s subscription. “At Bending Spoons, we acquire companies with the expectation of owning and operating them indefinitely, and we look forward to realizing Vimeo’s full potential as we reach new heights together,” Luca Ferrari, the CEO and co-founder of Bending Spoons, said in the press release.

articles.title: Bending Spoons is buying AOL for some reason
articles.summary: The Italian software company Bending Spoons is acquiring AOL after securing a $2.8 billion debt package.
articles.body: AOL will soon have a new owner. Bending Spoons, the Italian software company that has bought up a range of other digital businesses like Evernote, MeetUp, WeTransfer, and soon Vimeo, announced plans to purchase AOL from Yahoo after securing a $2.8 billion debt financing package. Over the past couple of decades, AOL has been passed from company to company, merging with Time Warner in 2001 before getting spun off and sold to Verizon in 2015 for $4.4 billion. Verizon merged AOL and Yahoo into a new company, called Oath, which it offloaded to private equity firm Apollo Global Management for around $5 billion in 2021. AOL was placed under the Yahoo umbrella following the acquisition. AOL still offers a web portal and email service, though it recently shut down dial-up internet service after more than three decades. Bending Spoons has made a flurry of acquisitions in recent years, a few of which were followed by layoffs and, in some cases, higher prices for customers. The company expects its acquisition of AOL to close by the end of this year, with CEO Luca Ferrari saying that Bending Spoons will “invest significantly to help the product and business flourish.” Even though it’s hard not to think about which company will acquire AOL next, Ferrari says in the press release that Bending Spoons has “never sold an acquired business,” and will serve AOL’s “large, loyal customer base for many years to come.”

articles.title: The TikTok deal is done, finally
articles.summary: The Trump admin deal transferring TikTok in the US to a new joint venture with Silver Lake, Oracle, and MGX as managing investors is done.
articles.body: Just over a year after it briefly disappeared from app stores, TikTok in the US is now part of a new entity, TikTok USDS Joint Venture LLC. With approval from both the US and China closing on the schedule laid out in December, ByteDance’s ownership of the new joint venture is now only 19.9 percent to satisfy the terms of the divest-or-ban law signed in 2024 by President Biden. The other 80.1 percent is owned by investment firm Silver Lake, Oracle, and Abu Dhabi investment firm MGX — the three “managing investors” that now hold 15 percent stakes — and several other smaller investors, like Michael Dell’s family investment firm. A press release announcing the deal’s closure didn’t say how much those stakes cost or give details about potentially launching a new app in the US. It did say that the joint venture’s oversight of “comprehensive data protections, algorithm security, content moderation, and software assurances for U.S. users” will apply to TikTok, the video editor CapCut, Lemon8, and “a portfolio” of other apps and services. For now, most of what we know is about the joint venture’s seven-member board, which includes TikTok US CEO Shou Zi Chew, and its first executive appointments, with TikTok’s former head of operations and trust and safety, Adam Presser, now serving as CEO. TikTok USDS: > Interoperability enables the Joint Venture to provide U.S. users with a global TikTok experience, ensuring U.S. creators can be discovered and businesses can operate on a global scale. TikTok global’s U.S. entities will manage global product interoperability and certain commercial activities, including e-commerce, advertising, and marketing. > TikTok USDS Joint Venture’s mandate is to secure U.S. user data, apps and the algorithm through comprehensive data privacy and cybersecurity measures. It will safeguard the U.S. content ecosystem through robust trust and safety policies and content moderation while ensuring continuous accountability through transparency reporting and third-party certifications. > Data Protection: U.S. user data will be protected by USDS Joint Venture in Oracle’s secure U.S. cloud environment. The Joint Venture will operate a comprehensive data privacy and cybersecurity program that is audited and certified by third party cybersecurity experts. The program will adhere to major industry standards, including the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) CSF and 800-53 and ISO 27001 as well as the Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) Security Requirements for Restricted Transactions. > Algorithm Security: The Joint Venture will retrain, test, and update the content recommendation algorithm on U.S. user data. The content recommendation algorithm will be secured in Oracle’s U.S. cloud environment. > Software Assurance: The Joint Venture will secure U.S. apps through software assurance protocols, and review and validate source code on an ongoing basis, assisted by its Trusted Security Partner, Oracle. > Trust & Safety: The Joint Venture will safeguard the U.S. content ecosystem and have decision-making authority for trust and safety policies and content moderation. > TikTok USDS Joint Venture has three managing investors, Silver Lake, Oracle and MGX, each holding 15%. Completing the full consortium of investors are: Dell Family Office, the investment firm of Michael Dell, Founder, Chairman and CEO of Dell Technologies; Vastmere Strategic Investments, LLC, an affiliate of Susquehanna International Group, LLP; Alpha Wave Partners; Revolution; Merritt Way, LLC controlled and managed by partners of Dragoneer; Via Nova, an affiliate of General Atlantic; Virgo LI, Inc., investment arm of a foundation established by Yuri and Julia Milner in support of science; and NJJ Capital, the family office of Xavier Niel, a French entrepreneur and pioneer in telecommunications. ByteDance retains 19.9% of the Joint Venture.

articles.title: Some feared an AI attack. The real reason for tech outages is more complicated
articles.summary: A string of technology outages across the country has the public quickly pointing fingers at artificial intelligence as fears swirl over a so-called doomsday. Researchers and public officials are suggesting AI was a likely factor — but not in the way people initially suspected. After days of uncertainty over the outages, national security officials in…
articles.body:
A string of technology outages across the country has the public quickly pointing fingers at artificial intelligence as fears swirl over a so-called doomsday. Researchers and public officials are suggesting AI was a likely factor — but not in the way people initially suspected.

After days of uncertainty over the outages, national security officials in the Trump administration told lawmakers on Wednesday the incidents were not due to cyberattacks but the simultaneous patching and upgrading of legacy systems.

Cybersecurity experts similarly said they so far found no evidence of coordinated malicious activity. Instead, some suggested AI’s rapid detection of new security vulnerabilities is causing various organizations to simultaneously upgrade and implement emergency patches that may not undergo full testing.

The incidents and the subsequent panic underscore a new reality of AI — one where the technology is demonstrating advanced ways to detect vulnerabilities in software and systems, while also causing temporary disruptions at the same time.

“It is easy to treat the emerging technology landscape and AI in particular as a scapegoat here, and there are certainly things that are very difficult for us to do as humans, but we’ve known for a very long time that there are challenges in the software supply chain,” Randy Rose, vice president of security operations at the Center for Internet Security (CIS), said in a media briefing Wednesday.

“There’s this kind of compounding thing that’s happening,” Rose added. “You have this accelerated AI-assisted vulnerability discovery, and you have this modernization that’s happening at the same time.”

Over the course of the past six days, outages hit various sectors, including banks, tech companies Microsoft and Apple and various government agencies. An outage at the Federal Aviation Administration led to a rare hours-long, nationwide ground stop last week, while the National Security Agency’s classified network also went down on Monday.

The simultaneous events across different industries sparked a flurry of panicked reactions online and in Washington, where lawmakers and pundits across the aisle pressed the Trump administration for answers on whether the events were related.

Amid the confusion, users online speculated the hypothetical “AI doomsday” that some of the technology’s researchers warned about had arrived, while others said they were stocking up on food and essentials in case of an infrastructure blackout.

A White House official on Wednesday said the administration’s assessment found the outages were “the result of upgrades of the systems being patched, hardware being applied,” and there is “no indication” of a cyberattack. Pointing to the companies’ stated reasons for the outages, the official said the causes are all “in the upgrading and patching realm.”

Concerns over the role of AI in the cyber world follow months of statements from Silicon Valley leaders who repeatedly warned how the technology’s capabilities could be used as both a tool to bolster U.S. infrastructure and a weapon for bad actors to exploit vulnerabilities.

After OpenAI disclosed its AI agents breached a testing environment and broke into the systems of the tech firm Hugging Face, numerous AI firms began publicly discussing similar incidents.

Vulnerability disclosures hit a record high in 2026, Rose said, but other experts said some of this is likely because AI is finding vulnerabilities that went undiscovered for years.

“Most vulnerabilities never get exploited … but we’re finding a lot of them now, and so there’s a lot of news about that kind of stuff, and that makes people worried about these kinds of things,” Nick Carroll, a cyber incident response manager at the national security firm Nightwing, told The Hill.

“It’s really just that we now have the tools that are able to actually go through this code in a way people traditionally have not had time to dig through and find all of those things,” Carroll continued.

Carroll noted the simultaneous nature of the incidents is just a matter of “unfortunate coincidences,” but he also pointed to the time of year, during which companies and teams are trying to upgrade platforms before the holidays and the year’s end.

“Everybody starts to rush, things kind of go wrong,” he said.

The rush to emergency patch newly discovered vulnerabilities could also be a factor in the recent spike in outages, experts suggested.

Before the increased use of AI, Carroll explained companies used to have a “very lengthy window” to test emergency patches, but “that’s starting to dry up for a lot of organizations,” as hackers use AI to exploit vulnerabilities more easily.

“The simple explanation is we’re finding more vulnerabilities (and faster) with AI. Fixing them is still hard and a completely different story,” Josh Bressers, the director of coordinated vulnerability disclosure at the firm VulnCheck, wrote in a LinkedIn post.

“The reality is security teams have been feeling the pressure from this onslaught all year,” Bressers wrote. “We’re well past the point of being able to ‘patch faster,’ and the uncomfortable truth is this is the new normal for the foreseeable future. Even if the volume levels off, it will be beyond what teams can handle.”

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency published a warning Tuesday that a critical vulnerability was discovered in common programming language Java.

The startup Calif, which used AI to discover the PHP vulnerability last month, said it used AI to discover the Java vulnerability. Java is used by nearly all of the Fortune 500 companies.

“It is the beating heart of the modern economy,” Calif wrote in a blog post Tuesday. “Banking, aviation, telecommunications, nearly every critical sector runs on Java, including national security systems.”

It is not clear whether the Java vulnerability played a role in the recent outages, though Oracle released a patch Tuesday.

Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, sought to quell concerns over the agency’s systems during The Hill’s “Red, Flight & Blue: Future of U.S. Aviation” event Wednesday. The agency cited a router in Arkansas that needed an upgrade, along with a Texas radar facility that caused a data flood.

“The system is absolutely safe,” Bedford told The Hill, while acknowledging, “We do have reliability challenges with our legacy systems.”

Regardless of AI’s role, cyber experts stressed companies should take away the need to bolster their security from the design phase of a product.

“The security best practices still stand,” Phyllis Lee, CIS’s vice president of security best practices, said. “It makes it even more important to implement a cybersecurity framework.”

articles.title: Policymakers view Anthropic’s looming IPO with wary eye
articles.summary: Lawmakers are watching Anthropic’s stock market debut with a wary eye, as the AI giant prepares for a massive initial public offering (IPO) at a moment of upheaval and uncertainty for the industry. Anthropic is poised to make its public debut Thursday in what is widely expected to be one of the biggest IPOs of the year. But…
articles.body:
Lawmakers are watching Anthropic’s stock market debut with a wary eye, as the AI giant prepares for a massive initial public offering (IPO) at a moment of upheaval and uncertainty for the industry.

Anthropic is poised to make its public debut Thursday in what is widely expected to be one of the biggest IPOs of the year. But it comes at a tumultuous moment, as the industry is still reeling from the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and grappling with the potentially existential risks of AI.

“The pressure to deliver profits will be immediate, and it will be immense. As a Congressman, the founder of the Monopoly Busters Caucus, and Patriot, I have a LOT of questions,” Rep. Pat Ryan (D-N.Y.) wrote in a post on the social platform X.

“I’m not writing this because I doubt the technology is powerful. I’m writing this because I’m terrified of the choices Anthropic will make to justify their valuation,” he added.

Anthropic is aiming to raise more than $64 billion at a valuation of about $1.4 trillion for its IPO, according to the company’s most recent filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).

This would put it on track to be the second largest public debut on record, behind only SpaceX’s massive debut earlier this year.

Major AI companies are looking to tap into public markets to help fund the costly endeavor of securing the vast computing power needed to support AI development.

OpenAI also confidentially filed to go public in June, around the same time Anthropic took its first step toward an IPO. But the ChatGPT maker has signaled a slower timeline than its competitor, aiming for a 2027 debut instead.

“We plan to be a public company at some point,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday. “There’s many reasons why that’s the right thing to do.”

“I do think that these recent months have been a newly challenging period, and there will be newly challenging periods ahead of us for a long time about the safety requirements in front of us,” he continued.

Altman previously told Fortune magazine in September that “given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public.”

His comments came at a moment when the top AI firms were dealing with a series of high-profile incidents in which AI agents went rogue, breaching outside organizations or acting in other unexpected ways.

Concerns about AI safety ratcheted up further when several AI researchers came out with warnings about the technology’s potentially catastrophic risks.

Anthropic acknowledged these risks in its SEC filing, noting that its models “have in the past behaved, and may in the future behave, in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking harmful actions that no user or third party directed.” CEO Dario Amodei was among the first AI leaders who called to “ slow the pace ” of the technology’s development amid the raft of safety warnings in September.

The company, which has prided itself on being a safety-focused AI firm, also recognized concerns that advanced AI systems could “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

This has left some lawmakers with more questions than answers ahead of the IPO.

“They’ve made very, very clear public statements that the technology they’re developing is potentially dangerous,” Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) told The Hill on Wednesday.

“Yet at the same time, they plan to proceed to take the company public, so that the people who work there make enormous sums of money to develop a product that they themselves say is dangerous,” he continued. “That makes no sense whatsoever.”

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) raised concerns Wednesday that Anthropic has failed “to answer for the potential threats to Americans’ retirements and the entire financial system if this IPO goes awry.”

She has previously underscored the risks to the financial system given the massive size of the IPO and the highly interconnected nature of the AI industry — which is already under pressure over its heavy reliance on debt financing and the recent Nvidia spy scandal that prompted Huang to resign.

Ryan questioned how being a public company could impact Anthropic’s motivations and decisions, such as its current choice to keep Claude ad-free.

“So what happens, for example, if they decide that they’re leaving money on the table by not selling ad space?” the New York Democrat said. “Think about every piece of information someone puts in Claude.”

“The stuff you wouldn’t even tell Google. Your SSN. Your credit card PIN. Your health records. Your relationship fears. You trust a profit-seeking corporation to just sit on that forever?”

He raised similar concerns about the firm’s commitment to safety in the face of profit pressures.

“Anthropic promised to stand up for their values ‘at critical points, even when this is costly for us commercially.’ That’s admirable,” Ryan added. “My question is: why the f— is that up to a handful of billionaires, without any input from the American people?”

State and local officials are also watching the Claude maker’s IPO closely.

A group of state treasurers and comptrollers from Maryland, Illinois, Connecticut, Colorado, New Mexico and Vermont sent a letter to Amodei last week, pressing him about “the potential negative impact of Anthropic’s proposed offering on the long-term stability of financial markets.”

They called on the AI firm to publicly address AI safety and risk management, the company’s governance structure and its approach to financial projections in the wake of a potential slowdown in development.

New York City Comptroller Mark Levine, who urged Anthropic last month to pause its IPO, said Wednesday that the company’s decision to move forward is “very disappointing.”

“We have a company that acknowledges their technology could lead to ‘catastrophic risk,’ and they themselves have called for pacing the frontier,” Levine told Bloomberg.

“So now it’s kind of a contradiction that this very company is going public now, raising capital that will help them accelerate their development and taking on all the pressure for growth and profitability that will weigh against the safety work,” he continued.

But some policymakers are more sanguine about Anthropic’s public debut.

“Anthropic has been one of the more responsible players in terms of realizing you’ve got to have mandatory AI safety rules,” Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.) said Wednesday, when asked about the upcoming IPO.

Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.), for his part, is leaving it up to the market.

“The market is going to tell us, and indeed it is telling us right now, the free market, what it thinks about AI infrastructure and how it’s being financed,” he told reporters Monday. “And right now, the market is obviously concerned.”

articles.title: Measles comeback puts daycares, schools on the front lines
articles.summary: Daycares and schools have a fight on their hands to keep students healthy after the U.S. officially lost its measles elimination status this week. As the highly contagious disease makes a comeback and vaccination rates dwindle, classrooms are prime targets for measles to spread. “Measles is perhaps the most infectious disease on the planet. If…
articles.body:
Daycares and schools have a fight on their hands to keep students healthy after the U.S. officially lost its measles elimination status this week.

As the highly contagious disease makes a comeback and vaccination rates dwindle, classrooms are prime targets for measles to spread.

“Measles is perhaps the most infectious disease on the planet. If a child with measles spends one hour in a classroom of 10 children at a daycare or school, nine of those children will catch measles,” said Lawrence Gostin, the director of the World Health Organization Collaborating Center on National and Global Health Law and a distinguished professor at Georgetown Law.

The U.S. lost its measles elimination status Tuesday after more than 25 years, with cases totaling more than 7,700 over the past two years and at least 10 deaths occurring so far this year.

At least two of the measles deaths in 2025 were from unvaccinated school-age children.

Public health officials and advocates have blamed the loss of the elimination status on lower vaccination rates.

The measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is typically required for public school students, but federal data showed that exemptions for vaccines among kindergartners over religious or other grounds hit an all-time high this year: 4.2 percent, up from 3.6 percent in 2025.

Only 92.4 percent of kindergarten students have received the MMR vaccine, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which sits below the 95 percent threshold for herd immunity.

“By law, children are required to attend school. With measles rising, we are forcing parents to send their children into unsafe classrooms. And all of this if fully preventable,” Gostin said.

When schools detect a case among students, they often have to notify anyone who is unvaccinated and exclude them from classrooms and other school-related activities.

Last month, an entire school building had to be shut down because of a measles outbreak in Pennsylvania, which on Wednesday confirmed its eighth measles death of the year.

“It’s especially important to think about this for our daycares, especially those daycares that see infants under the age of 1,” said Kisha Davis, president of the American Academy of Family Physicians.

“Those younger kids don’t have that protection, and so it’s really important for everyone around them to be vaccinated. Those kids, especially, benefit from herd immunity … as well as other kids who may be immunocompromised or have other conditions that prevent them from being able to be vaccinated,” she added.

Measles can stay in the air for up to two hours, making classrooms and daycares an easy setting for it to spread quickly among unvaccinated people.

The MMR shot is found to be 97 percent effective at combating measles and was credited with being the reason the U.S. eliminated the disease in 2000.

But vaccine skepticism has grown, and Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the head of the Department of Health and Human Services, has sent mixed messages about inoculation efforts.

After the elimination status loss was announced Tuesday, Kennedy recommended that everyone get the MMR vaccine in a social media post, despite previously suggesting breaking up the shot schedule.

“We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles,” Kennedy said.

“Worldwide COVID-era disruptions interrupted routine childhood vaccination, leaving gaps in protection here and abroad. The multi-year global outbreak has caused many nations to lose their elimination status including, Armenia, Austria, Azerbaijan, Bolivia, Canada, Mexico, Spain, United Kingdom, and Uzbekistan,” he added.

Experts say it is important for schools and doctors to reach out to vaccine-skeptical parents with respect and engage in conversations in good faith.

“I find that when I have an honest conversation with my patients and let them express what their frustration is or what their worry is and then talk about the benefits that they may not have heard about, we often get to a place of vaccination,” Davis said. “And so, I think approaching those conversations not from shame or blame, but more from respect and honesty, really does go a long way to help people be more comfortable with making the decision to get their kids vaccinated.”

But some advocates believe vaccine requirements should be stronger, with only medical exemptions available instead of the religious or philosophical ones that some states allow.

With measles back, experts fear the return of other diseases the U.S. thought were gone.

“Losing the nation status may signal that the U.S. is vulnerable to more vaccine-preventable diseases. Measles is what we call the canary in the coal mine when it comes to vaccine-preventable diseases. It’s usually the first to break, and then it signals that we’re vulnerable to others,” said Caitlin Gilmet, communications director for American Families for Vaccines.

articles.title: Watch: The Hill’s Capitol Crypto Forum
articles.summary: A new generation of financial infrastructure is taking shape through the development of blockchain networks and dollar-backed tokens known as stablecoins. While the House voted to advance the Digital Asset Market…
articles.body:
A new generation of financial infrastructure is taking shape through the development of blockchain networks and dollar-backed tokens known as stablecoins.

Central to this evolution is the Clarity Act — a comprehensive landmark bill that would create a U.S. regulatory framework for the cryptocurrency industry.

While the House voted to advance the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act more than a year ago, it is stalled in the Senate. A tight legislative calendar, partisan ethics debates surrounding crypto business involvement by government officials and ongoing friction between traditional banks and the crypto sector over stablecoin rewards and decentralized finance regulation have all slowed momentum.

To explore what comes next, The Block and The Hill are joining forces to host the inaugural Capitol Crypto Forum on Nov. 19th in Washington, D.C. For the first time following the midterms , lawmakers will gather with regulators and the blockchain industry to take a deep dive into what’s to come for digital assets.

Why is it important to bring digital-asset activity into a regulated U.S. framework? What are the major hurdles preventing passage? Why and how is passing the Clarity Act best for U.S. national security? What happens if it doesn’t pass? What are next steps for key regulators such as the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission? What happens next for crypto legislation in a new Congress?

Join us as we bridge the gap between Capitol Hill and the crypto ecosystem to map out the path forward for U.S. digital asset policy.

The event is scheduled to begin at 8:15 a.m. EST.

articles.title: Cassidy rejects Trump nominee to lead National Science Foundation
articles.summary: A key Senate committee rejected the Trump administration’s pick to lead the National Science Foundation (NSF), just hours after the White House decided to withdraw its nominee to lead the Food and Drug Administration. Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, on Wednesday said Jim O’Neill, who previously…
articles.body:
A key Senate committee rejected the Trump administration’s pick to lead the National Science Foundation (NSF), just hours after the White House decided to withdraw its nominee to lead the Food and Drug Administration.

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, on Wednesday said Jim O’Neill, who previously served as acting director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and deputy secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), would not be considered to lead the NSF.

If he had been confirmed, O’Neill would have led the agency for six years. But Cassidy at the beginning of a meeting to vote on nominees said O’Neill didn’t have the support to advance and the vote had been canceled.

O’Neill “did not do enough to stand up for science and against irresponsible decisions and statements” from Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Cassidy said.

“His role in the firing of Dr. Susan Monarez raised further concerns about the independent judgment he would bring to NSF,” Cassidy continued. “Several of the committee members had those concerns.”

Susan Monarez was ousted as CDC director in 2025 just one month after she was confirmed, a move she attributed to her refusal to rubber-stamp vaccine recommendations from Kennedy that lacked evidence or to fire employees without cause.

After Monarez was fired, O’Neill briefly became acting CDC director while continuing to serve as the No. 2 official at HHS. He was then replaced as part of an agencywide shake-up and nominated for the NSF post.

“I like Jim personally, but this time requires leadership and fortitude and standing up for what is right,” Cassidy said Wednesday.

O’Neill does not have a science background. Prior to joining the administration, he worked extensively for venture capitalist Peter Thiel.

The NSF is an independent agency that funds basic research. It has been without a Senate-confirmed leader since April 2025, when Sethuraman Panchanathan, who was appointed during President Trump’s first term, resigned amid the Trump administration’s effort to cancel hundreds of millions of dollars of active grants and slash agency funding.

In April, Trump removed every member of the National Science Board, NSF’s presidentially appointed oversight body.

Cassidy, a physician, lost his primary earlier this year to a Trump-backed challenger.

He has come under intense criticism from public health leaders for casting the deciding vote in committee and on the Senate floor to confirm Kennedy.

Cassidy on Wednesday said his committee would have endorsed Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration despite concerns about her role in the Trump administration’s vaccine policy, but the White House withdrew her nomination before the vote.

articles.title: Unless you’re building a data center or have a side hustle, you’re significantly worse off than last year, according to the Fed
articles.summary: “Consumer resilience continues to depend on lowering savings rates and engaging in side hustles. It implies labor cost pressures are not an inflation driver,...
articles.body:
Visit a grocery store or gas station, and you'll notice prices across the U.S. keep climbing. On top of that, the Federal Reserve's latest minutes suggest that unless you're in two very niche groups of consumers, you're probably markedly worse off in terms of income in 2026 compared with last year. By its very nature, inflation erodes spending power as prices rise. But in a balanced economy, when inflation is at its target of 2%, those increases are offset by income growth, so consumers can still afford goods and services without seeking additional income or eating into their savings. But in 2026, inflation has been well above the 2% target. The latest inflation readings from the Bureau of Labor Statistics came in at 3.7% over the past 12 months, through September 2026. However, in addition to prices rising above the central bank's 2% target, Fed minutes from the latest Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting showed wage growth for most industries lagged well behind price increases.

The affordability conundrum facing households is therefore twofold: Not only are prices rising quicker than consumers can reasonably expect, but any increases to their income are coming in well short of the new demands on their purse strings.

The Fed minutes from the meeting ended Oct. 28 read that most participants "judged that aggregate nominal wage growth remained moderate and was broadly consistent with the committee's 2% inflation objective."

Some sectors are posting wage growth, the minutes noted: Many members "observed that shortages of skilled workers needed for data center construction and related industries had contributed to sizable wage premiums in those industries, while a few noted that reduced labor supply in industries reliant on immigrant workers could add to sectoral wage pressures, although these developments did not appear to be having a material effect on aggregate wage measures."

These factors are potentially good news for the Fed because they suggest the U.S. is not on the cusp of an inflationary wage-price spiral—making it easier for the FOMC to bring inflation back to its mandated 2% target. A wage-price spiral refers to a feedback loop in which higher labor costs push up production and consumer demand, leading workers to demand higher incomes again to offset the increased cost of living.

However, while it's one less headache for the Fed, incomes lagging inflation by nearly 2% means consumers already stretched are being spread even thinner.

"Fed members acknowledged that wage growth is consistent with their inflation target—but inflation is not consistent with their target," noted UBS chief economist Paul Donovan to clients this morning. "This is a subtle way of saying that wages are falling behind inflation."

articles.title: Traders Are Betting on Interest Rates Staying High for Years
articles.summary: Traders are betting that major central banks will keep interest rates largely unchanged for years once they’ve finished hiking at the end of 2027.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Traders are betting that major central banks will keep interest rates largely unchanged for years once they've finished hiking at the end of 2027.

Money markets began 2026 pricing in rate cuts by the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of England but had to pivot when the Iran war throttled oil supplies, lifting inflation. Traders flipped to betting on a series of hikes, while also wagering that easing would follow next year.

Those hopes for lower borrowing costs have almost vanished as the conflict drags on and a wave of investment in technology, rearmament and the energy transition boosts competition for funding, fueling higher bond yields. All three central banks are expected to raise rates further in the next 12 months, and then mostly sit tight at least until 2031, based on interest rate futures.

"I call this the yield era," said Bob Stoutjesdijk, investment strategy and portfolio manager at Osmosis Investment Management. "We are living in a world of structurally higher rates of inflation."

Companies went on a borrowing binge to finance investment in artificial intelligence this year, hitting the market with a record flood of bonds and hoovering up hundreds of billions of dollars. There's much more debt to come in 2027, according to JPMorgan Chase & Co., which sees big tech spending, and elevated refinancing needs, driving another record year of US investment-grade bond issuance.

Many Fed policymakers view the AI buildout as a material source of inflation risk, according to minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee's October meeting published this week.

In addition, governments are ratcheting up spending on defense and infrastructure, most notably in Germany, which is set to be the largest gross issuer of debt among euro area peers next year, according to strategists at Commerzbank AG.

To be sure, oil prices have retreated from a six-month peak in recent weeks, but inflation numbers are still hot, fueling wagers on more rate hikes against a volatile geopolitical backdrop.

"Macro and political uncertainty remain elevated," said Christoph Rieger, head of rates and credit research at Commerzbank.

articles.title: Senate Democrat: Trump administration not creating ‘air of confidence’ with response to outages
articles.summary: Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) said the Trump administration is not inspiring confidence among the public with their responses to recent widespread technology outages that the country has been grappling with. “The president and his administration need to be actively trying to encourage confidence,” Gallego said during an appearance on CNN. “This is not a partisan…
articles.body:
Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) said the Trump administration is not inspiring confidence among the public with their responses to recent widespread technology outages that the country has been grappling with.

“The president and his administration need to be actively trying to encourage confidence,” Gallego said during an appearance on CNN. “This is not a partisan thing. This is not me trying to be a bad Democrat or a good Democrat to attack Republicans.”

“I want the American public to have confidence right now. And these guys are not creating an air of confidence whatsoever,” he added.

In the past week, Americans experienced technology outages across industries that impacted flights, banking systems, emails and more.

On Nov. 12, Microsoft faced global outages that impacted its flagship platforms Outlook and Teams. The incident, which lasted about a day, was “introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” the company said.

One day later, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop that lasted more than four hours. Authorities attributed the incident to an overload of data on routers. Thousands of flights were delayed and canceled on Friday, impacting operations through the weekend.

On Monday, customers of several banks including Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo had trouble accessing their accounts. A spokesperson from JPMorgan Chase told The Hill the cause was “a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems” and denied anything “cyber-related.”

Chase said on the social platform X on Thursday that “third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack.”

“Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses. There is no disruption to our services. Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring,” the company added.

Trump administration officials, including Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, have repeatedly said the outages are not linked to cyberattacks. Mullin recently said super intelligence , the administration’s preferred name for artificial intelligence, could be the reason behind the outages.

President Trump, on Tuesday, weighed in on the outages, saying “it’s fine.”

“It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and have all the money, things like that happen,” the president said.

Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt advised officials to spread their message “ wide and loud .”

Leavitt said “there should be a message directly to the American people” from either Trump or a White House official explaining “what they know and what they believe to be true to really calm the temperature.”

images.caption: Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) addresses reporters following the weekly policy luncheon on Nov. 10, 2026.

articles.title: How Silicon Valley lost the public, with Crooked Media’s Jon Favreau
articles.summary: The Crooked Media cofounder on the midterms, the tech right’s reckoning, running a creator business at the mercy of the algorithm, and why AI is the ultimate collective action problem.
articles.body: Today, I’m talking with Jon Favreau, a political commentator and cofounder of Crooked Media. You probably know Jon best from a little show called Pod Save America, which Jon started with a group of fellow Obama staffers in the wake of Donald Trump’s election in 2016. It’s now one of the most popular podcasts in the country. Since then, Pod Save America and the company created around it, Crooked, have become one of the major success stories of independent liberal media. So one of my central questions for Jon was why he thought Democrats swept the midterms earlier this month and, more importantly, why it happened now — especially after a wave of tech billionaires made big swings to the right while buying huge pillars of the information ecosystem. That’s Elon Musk buying Twitter and turning it into X, Mark Zuckerberg sucking up to Trump while tearing down Meta’s content moderation infrastructure, the Ellison family buying stakes in TikTok, turning over the leadership of CBS News and now potentially CNN while integrating Warner into Skydance… the list goes on. How did they all miss the huge swing in the mood of the public — or, more apocalyptically, fail in their attempts to control the media and thus influence the public? --- [Image: Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. --- Crooked itself is also just a fascinating business, as all creator businesses are. When we think of what you might call news creators, we tend to look to the right — after all, conservative media have been building an alternative, direct-to-consumer pipeline since the dawn of talk radio. But Jon and his fellow Crooked cofounders created a reliable template for liberal creators, and it’s working. Crooked hired its first CEO a few years ago, now offers more than a dozen original shows, and has a staff of around 100 people working on everything from live events to political advocacy. Jon tells me the subscription business has crossed 65,000 members. So of course I wanted to know how Jon feels about topics we cover a lot here on Decoder: online distribution, the platform power of YouTube, and how you balance running a media business that has to make money with a newsroom that, ultimately, has a political mission and a strong point of view. Of course, AI. Jon has turned his own podcast Offline into something close to an AI policy show this year. He has a lot of thoughts on how Congress should tackle the issue. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Jon Favreau, the co-host of Pod Save America and cofounder of Crooked Media. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Jon Favreau, you’re the co-host of Pod Save America, you’re the host of Offline. You’re also the co-founder of Crooked Media. Welcome to Decoder. Thanks for having me, Nilay. I’m excited to have you here. I’ve been on Offline with you. It was a really fun conversation. I have a million ideas about what to talk about with you. I want to talk about Crooked as a creator company in this particular moment in media. I feel like we have to start with the midterms though. The blue tsunami is here. It feels like a repudiation of the billionaires owning all the social platforms, the billionaires owning all the broadcast networks. What do you make of that? I’ve just been turning this over in my head that the media was purchased in a huge and meaningful way, and Americans said, “No, we still see through it.” I think it’s a repudiation of a government that came into power with the chief promise of bringing inflation down and making life more affordable, and it didn’t do that. If you’ve looked at the last couple of elections, people voted a party into power and they said, “Everything’s too expensive and I want stuff to be cheaper and I don’t want to be struggling. Can you do something about it?” And then either they try to do something about it or they fail to do something about it or like Trump, you don’t even try at all. You actually make life harder, and then people say, “The propaganda that’s coming out of Fox or any of these right-wing platforms doesn’t matter. I fill up my car and gas is expensive and I don’t know if I’m ever going to be able to afford a house because interest rates are up, et cetera, et cetera.” You can say whatever you want to say, but people’s lived experiences end up being more salient than the messages that they get from politics. Is it just that simple? I hate that it’s that simple. It’s just, “Gas prices are up, just throw the bums out.” But I would say the last 10 years of politics are, “Can I tweak policy into reality?” We’ve seen it happen several times. “Can I wage memetic warfare on the American public until these Republican talking points are the framework in which all further conversation must happen?” We’ve seen it happen on the left too. I think Defund the Police is a great example of a thing that just spiraled out of control and maybe turned an election. But in particular, we’re going to wake up and the Fox News machine is going to define the terms of the debate, and then we’re going to wake up and whatever’s happening on Twitter is going to define the terms of the debate. That has been how it’s worked for an awfully long time, and “the gas prices are too high” and “this war is stupid” maybe just defeated it. It works to a point, but there are certain conditions that messaging and media just can’t overcome, especially for the party in power or forever, whoever’s running the White House. The same was true with Joe Biden. Joe Biden could go out there and say, “We passed this bill. We gave money out. We gave the checks out and things are getting better and we’re just recovering from Covid. You haven’t felt it yet, but it’s getting better and look at the economic statistics.” And people just said, “No, I don’t feel that yet. So I’m going to maybe give Donald Trump another try, even though I think he’s a shitty guy and I don’t like him very much.” But maybe they remember the economy of the first term being good. We dealt with this when Obama ran and became president in 2009. They thought, “Financial crisis. Can’t stand Bush anymore. I’m going to try Obama.” And then Obama gets into office and for the first two years, the financial crisis is over, but the recession is still there. People are still out of work. So they said, “I know you passed healthcare and I know you passed the recovery act, but I still can’t find a job. The economy just still doesn’t feel great to me. So it doesn’t matter what you say you did or how great your messaging is, I don’t feel it. I’m going to vote in a Republican Congress.” It’s been like that for as long as I’ve been in politics. Is there some reason the incumbent party does not realize that saying something that sounds like “the fundamentals of the economy are strong” kills you? Because you’re describing a pattern that repeats and it’s that phrase almost exactly. Yes. That’s why we understood it once 2012 rolled around because people were still not satisfied with the economy when Obama was running for reelection and we did everything we could to make that election a choice. We acknowledged that people were still struggling and people were still in pain. We totally avoided the long list of statistics about how wonderful the economy was getting and how everyone had recovered and all that kind of stuff. We just said, “Look, things are still rough out there, but it’s a choice. This is the kind of vision Mitt Romney has for the economy and this is the vision we have for the economy. You get to pick one.” There’s a way, if you are the incumbent party in power, to still keep people on your side, but you’ve got to at least acknowledge and be honest about how people are feeling. You can’t tell people to feel a way that they aren’t feeling. You can’t tell people that a whole bunch of issues are important that aren’t the issues that matter most to them in their lives or at least to most people, which is, “Do I feel economically secure and do I actually feel safe?” That’s why people care about crime and they care about safety in their communities and then they also care about whether they can afford gas and groceries. The one issue that really struck me in that framework is surveillance. We’ve done a number of episodes about Flock cameras and AI-enabled surveillance and the idea that you can just link all the databases together and Palantir can send a drone to your house to murder you. That connects directly to safety. The CEO of Ring has been on the show and his argument is, “If I put up enough Ring cameras, I will zero out crime in certain neighborhoods.” I’ve asked him about the mechanism of how that will exactly work and the answer is that the thieves will be deterred by surveillance. It’s the same for the CEO of Flock. It’s the same argument everywhere. “If we just watch you enough, we’ll stop crime.” The American public hates this idea. There’s some limit to how much crime-stopping you want compared to how much surveillance must occur. I watched the CEO of Flock in particular try to go hard MAGA in this election cycle and use the phrase, “The radical leftists want a crime world,” or whatever it is he was saying, and it just didn’t work. That to me felt like a glimmer of a realignment where the libertarians in America were saying, “No, we still don’t want a state with this level of power,” and your classic ACLU Democrats were saying, “Yep, that’s pretty bad,” and then throw all the bumps out, like, “Just get out of here and we’ll start over.” What do you make of that? Because there are other glimmers of realignment, but that is the one that really stuck out to me. It’s interesting. I do think privacy is the other issue that affects people personally, that they can feel. You go through your life and if you lose your privacy, then there’s public shaming and embarrassment — there’s a violation there. So at least in people’s minds, they still do balance safety and security with privacy concerns. We have that in so many aspects of life. But you see with the Flock cameras, that’s also why Trump’s immigration policy has gone so poorly for them politically, because you have the same voters who say, “I think the border was a bit of a mess under Biden,” and even people who are welcoming to immigrants say, “I think there’s too many immigrants all at once coming over the border.” We didn’t know what to do. Public services were strained, especially in some of these border communities. The same people who wanted a more secure border suddenly looked around and said, “I also don’t want the government with masked, armed federal agents coming into my community and kidnapping people and taking them off the street and having that fear as I go about my day that I may be taken by the state just because of what I look like or how I talk or who I’m associated with. Or if I’m trying to protest the government, which is my constitutional right, then they might come after me then too.” It’s too early to tell if it’s a realignment, but I do think there’s this resistance to state power, or state overreach, that we haven’t seen the extent of in another administration in our lifetime, that is as bad as it’s been with Donald Trump in his second term. It is also that privacy, to some huge extent, is actually a free speech and First Amendment [issue]. We’ve seen this with FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. I keep calling him a dummy. I get all these notes saying, “Why do you call him dummy? He’s evil.” I’m saying, “No, because he’s dumb. This is strategically dumb. Fighting comedians is stupid. This is bad. Both sides will turn on him the second he doesn’t have a Donald Trump to protect him.” I think we’re going to see it. There are incoming members of Congress talking about FCC oversight today. But that one felt like another glimmer of, “Oh, this one party has gone too far. They own all the channels of speech. We are watching Elon Musk turn the moderation knobs however he wants it and the chairman of the FCC is attacking comedians. We don’t have to overthink this. We can just call this bad.” The third one is AI. It’s data centers where you see both sides coming together to say no. Something like 41 of 43 data center moratoriums passed. And that’s just classic American NIMBYism: “I just don’t want this loud building here.” What do you make of that one? It’s classic American NIMBYism, but it’s also this larger feeling that we’re losing control of the forces that shape our lives. Because when you talk to people who oppose the data centers, so much of it is about, “There was an NDA. It was all a secret. We couldn’t express our opposition to this before the deal was already done.” Part of it is connected to AI. Part of it is just, “My electricity bills are going up. It’s fucking noisy.” Any of the people who live around data centers, it’s unbelievably noisy. It’s bright in the middle of the night. In some cases, you see communities where the community has gotten together and said, “I don’t want a data center,” and the local politicians say they don’t want it and they get overruled and somehow the data center ends up there anyway. At least there’s been a turn there and that’s not happening as much anymore. But I do think there’s this feeling that, “We don’t want this in our community and yet more powerful companies and politicians are shoving it down our throats anyway, and we’re not going to take that because we should have control over what happens in our lives and what happens in our community.” We did a big story on Kevin O’Leary’s project in Utah. We reported it out and we were there. And we assumed he would talk to us because he talks to everybody. We got to the end and we sent our “no surprises” email and he sent his lawyers back at us and I thought, “Thank you for this incredible gift of threatening us.” Crazy. Threatening us with legal action for talking to people in Utah about his data center. But that’s the level of aggression that most of these big projects come with. Yes. Meta really loves talking about its project in Louisiana, but it doesn’t feel like the people in Louisiana felt like that was a choice they made. That was something Meta imposed on them and now the teachers got a raise and they need to be quiet. They don’t feel the need to explain the projects or the data centers to the community. Even the people who are very pro-data centers say, “There are a lot of conspiracy theories about data centers and all this opposition is based in propaganda. Actually you can build them so that they run on clean energy and that they pay for the power.” All of this might be true, but the companies — the hyperscalers, Meta and all these places that are trying to build these data centers — didn’t bother to try to explain the benefits. They didn’t bother to try to tell people in advance that this was happening or negotiate with communities. They’re doing it all now because of the pushback. But at the time, it was more, “You say that this is going to go great for us, but you also said social media was going to go great for us.” If you just look at the larger economy with AI, people said globalization was going to go great for people. People are tired of hearing from people in elite circles, whether it’s in business or government, who say, “This new technological advance in development is going to be great for everyone. Trust us and just let us do what we want and you’ll benefit at some point.” People just say, “No, I don’t trust you anymore.” Yeah, it’s funny. My hottest take continues to be that if consumer AI products were any good, these companies would have an easier time. Google’s AI overviews are not good enough to convince anyone to build a data center. Deepfake slop on Instagram is not going to convince anyone to build a data center. The best pitch they have is, “One day we’ll cure cancer,” but you might still have to navigate the healthcare system for that to happen to you. That seems pretty opaque. And then it’s like Salesforce will get better and an ultra-weaponized B2B SaaS environment is not going to do it. If you just put the Netflix logo on the side of the data center, people might calm down. They like Netflix, but there’s no consumer product that is making the sale. It’s just these guys and they don’t seem capable of doing it. No. And they continue to sit down for interviews and say, “Yeah, and it could kill everyone and it could do all that, but also there’s plenty of good that’s coming from it and we’ve got it covered. We’ve got it covered.” So to wrap this all up — and then I want to talk about Crooked and I want to talk about where we go from here — the thing that I was thinking about as I watched the election returns come in was at the beginning of Trump 2.0, there was a Steve Bannon quote that just ricocheted through my mind in our coverage. It was “politics is downstream of culture.” This is just the [Breitbart] thesis. I tend to believe Steve Bannon on this actually, that the cultural atmosphere of the country has some big effect on our politics. And then I watched the Trump administration engineer the sale or control of TikTok to Oracle and Larry Ellison. I watched CBS News get taken over by the Ellisons and Bari Weiss. I watched Elon Musk turn the knobs on X even harder. I watched the FCC work its way towards the removal of the restriction on broadcast ownership, so even fewer big companies could own more broadcast stations in the country. I thought, “Oh, the mechanisms of culture are bending their will to the Trump administration and this is going to lead to some permanent political outcome.” We covered it that way. Then this election happened, and that appears to have been totally wrong. I just got that wrong and I’m still trying to figure that out. Politics is downstream from culture, but material conditions rule out. As you are trying to form an opposition to the incumbent party — whatever it may be, and now it’s the Trump administration — culture is important to bringing people onto your side and building a movement and building an opposition that’s powerful enough to defeat the current incumbents. That’s going to be important. But in terms of whether you are the incumbent and whether you are the party in power and material conditions aren’t great, ultimately it doesn’t matter if you control the culture, or at least it doesn’t help you as much as people think it might because you can’t outrun material conditions. I wonder if that’s going to lead to a Woke 3.0. A former Verge reporter, Kylie Robison, tweeted at Jason Calacanis, “Put the pronouns in bio lil bro,” which is just one of the funniest reposts on election night that I saw. I’m wondering, do you think that there is a cultural pendulum swing coming, or is it straightforwardly “improve our material conditions”? Now, this could end up being naive, but I think that the left has grown over the decade and learned from the excesses of Woke 1.0. Did I say Woke 3.0? I meant Woke 2.0. [Laughs] Woke 2.0. My staff said this too. They were talking about Woke 3.0 and I said, “Guys, what happened to Woke 2.0?” Woke 2.0 is crypto. We don’t talk about that. I was asking them, “Where did Woke 2.0 go?” But, no, I do think that there’s tons of factional fighting in the Democratic Party as there always is. Sure. But there does seem to be broad agreement on making sure that the party focuses on people’s material conditions and affordability. You even see that acknowledgement on the right as well. JD Vance said that, Ted Cruz said that. So it’s on the mind of all the people who are going to run for president in 2028. The left is very cognizant, especially progressives, of what the culture wars and woke and all that kind of stuff cost them, fairly or unfairly. They don’t want to make that mistake again. Because I think everyone on the left, from the far left to the center left, understands the stakes in a way that we might not have when Trump first took office in 2016. I want to come back to that as we talk about the future of the media ecosystem, but this is a good place to talk about Crooked itself. You started Crooked in the Trump administration. It’s a product of the first Trump administration. It has grown to become a force. I have here in my notes that some people call you a kingmaker. It’s an honor to be in your presence. [Laughs] What king have we made? If you could make me one, that would be great. I think I’d be an excellent king of America. Tell me about Crooked. How is this company structured? How does it work? We started in 2016 as a podcast. When we were in the White House, Tommy Vietor, Jon Lovett and I had talked about how there’s not enough progressive media out there. Part of it is because people in progressive media, just like people in politics, take themselves too seriously. There’s not a lot of joking around because everything is “end of the world” kind of stuff. So, we thought, what if we had a progressive media company where we didn’t take ourselves too seriously, where we used humor to bring people along as well? That’s what we started in 2017, right when Trump took office, and then it has grown since then. I think we have 16 podcasts right now that are on. We have 65,000 paid subscribers, and we’ve got about 100 employees. We have Vote Save America, which is the advocacy arm of the company. It just raised a couple million dollars for this last cycle and asked people to run for office themselves who listened to the show. We had 2,000 people raise their hands to run for office this last cycle. A bunch of them won. Part of the theory when we started is we don’t want to just tell people what’s broken about the world, but give them the tools and information they need to fix it. There was advocacy built into the founding of the company. But somewhere around 2022, we finally decided that we need a CEO for this company. We need a real grownup. So we hired Lucinda Treat to be our CEO in 2022, and it has let the three of us focus on editorial and making content. Lucinda runs the company, and that has been a real blessing. Because running a company of 100 people is not something I’m good at, I would say. Yeah, I run a newsroom of like 50 and I’m still figuring it out every day. So 100 people, 16 podcasts — how is that basically organized? What’s the general structure there? Lucinda is the CEO, and under her we have a head of news and politics and a head of culture and entertainment. Just as every company has, we have finance and marketing, and people and culture. Vote Save America is headquartered in DC, and we have a few news folks in DC. We have some newsletters as well, because we’re on Substack now. We have two reporters who are in DC and covering stuff there. Now we’re expanding. We just launched Still Counting with Nate Silver, Clare Malone and Galen Druke, which is a reboot of FiveThirtyEight, and they’re in New York. So we now have a presence in New York as well. That’s the company, and over the last couple years we’ve been focusing a lot, as everyone has been, on YouTube and building the audience on YouTube. Every pod is a video pod now. We’re trying to grow the subscriber base as well so that we have balanced streams of revenue between advertising and subscribers. We’re in a real moment for creator-led media. I’m thinking of Andrew Sullivan warning the Republican Party of epistemic closure in 2000 on his blog on The Atlantic. And now we’ve landed at a closed podcast ecosystem where I’m pretty confident everyone’s buying views for each other, just to be clear, to make it look bigger and more influential than it is. But the fever has to break there too. The CEOs can’t all just be creators. They have to run their companies and make their shareholders money and operate in a new political environment. How does that fever break? Silicon Valley has always been incredibly insular like this. Even back in the social media age, even when we dealt with them in government. I got to know some of these folks afterwards when I moved out here. They view everyone who works in government as, “Politics is just an engineering problem to solve. The fact that it’s this messy means you must be a bunch of dummies running the place.” This is the theory behind DOGE. “If we can just go in there and bring our technology and bring our brilliance, we should solve all these political problems.” But political problems are problems of the human condition. It’s people trying to figure out how to live together and divvy up scarce resources and figure out how to govern themselves. That’s really messy and you actually need some social and political expertise to do that. You can’t just be a genius coder or a capitalist and feel like this is going to solve everything. But I think for a long, long time in Silicon Valley, they’ve seen the government as just another problem to be solved by engineering or capital allocation. And it’s just not. It’s never going to be that. Politics is going to be much messier. I think it’s all of that. And then one I would add to it is they also see it as a rich source of revenue, which is why you have seen so many of them move into being defense contractors. It’s an inarguable way to get a bunch of money from the government, to say, “We will build you weapons and AI systems for blah, blah, blah.” All of them have done it regardless of their professed values. The idea that YouTube is run by a defense contractor is mind-blowing to me. I know. But it is just straightforwardly true, right? Yeah. You can see the idea that SpaceX is a defense contractor and we might turn down Starlink in Ukraine and Trump has to go on television and be like, “I have no idea what happened.” Right, and Elon’s just sitting there saying, “I can flip a switch whenever I want.” Yeah, there’s something there. Again, to come back to collective action problems and the role of government to actually control these companies and control the industry. It seems like it’s up for grabs in a way that suggests you and I should probably talk again very soon. It feels like in these next two years, that realignment, the glimmers of it that I see are either going to come true or not. I’ve been wrong before, but something about the relationship between government and the tech industry is bound to change. I agree. Jon, this has been great. What’s next for Crooked? Tell people what to look out for. We just finished Crooked Con, which was wildly successful. Even though people have not announced their candidacies yet, by the time we get to winter, it’s going to be in full swing. So DeSantis, Rubio and JD. Ted Cruz. Oh, God. I know, and then a million people on the Democratic side. You’re already covering it. All right. I was hopeful that we would get some sincere legislative action, but we’re doing primaries. We’ll do both. It’s going to happen at the same time. I love it. Well, thank you so much for being undercover. This has been amazing. Thanks for having me. Questions or comments? articles.title: UK government forced to disclose secret Apple backdoor order | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The U.K. tribunal's ruling rejected London's claim that disclosing the order would be damaging to national security.
articles.body:
The U.K. government has been ordered to confirm that it issued a secret order demanding Apple to provide authorities with encrypted customer information.

The Thursday ruling from the U.K.’s Investigatory Powers Tribunal, an independent court that allows citizens to challenge government surveillance orders, is a rare rebuke for the government, which sought to keep the encryption backdoor order a state secret.

The tribunal’s ruling rejected the Home Office’s claim that disclosing the order would be damaging to national security.

The ruling comes a year after the U.K. government reportedly demanded that Apple build a backdoor to allow U.K. authorities access to customer data anywhere in the world. Details of the so-called “technical capabilities notice,” which are issued under strict non-disclosure rules, leaked to the media, which drew ire from White House officials and U.S. lawmakers who criticized the effort , arguing that the U.K. order would put Americans’ privacy at risk.

California-based Apple refused the order, and blocked U.K. users from switching on its Advanced Data Protection data-encryption feature for iCloud, rather than comply with the demand. The U.K.’s secret order was later narrowed to allow access to British nationals’ data stored in Apple’s encrypted cloud, and Apple also challenged this second order.

Prior to the ruling, Apple was legally barred from disclosing the order, even after details leaked. When reached for comment, Apple told TechCrunch that it welcomes the decision to make public the fact that the U.K. Home Office issued a technical capability notice.

Apple previously said that it has “never built a backdoor or master key” to any of its products or services and “never will.”

A spokesperson for the U.K. Home Office, which has yet to confirm the existence of a notice, did not respond to a request for comment.

Rights group Liberty International, which brought the legal challenge on behalf of two individuals, said that this is the first known time that the government has been compelled to confirm the existence of a secret technical order.

A final hearing on what specific order details can be released is anticipated next year.

articles.title: Musk: ‘There’s no one that can really replace’ Huang at Nvidia
articles.summary: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk reiterated his support for Jensen Huang, who recently resigned from his position as CEO of Nvidia after mounting scrutiny over reports of his extramarital affairs, one of which reportedly was with an alleged spy. “There’s no one that can really replace Jensen, I mean, he does the roles of several people,”…
articles.body:
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk reiterated his support for Jensen Huang, who recently resigned from his position as CEO of Nvidia after mounting scrutiny over reports of his extramarital affairs, one of which reportedly was with an alleged spy.

“There’s no one that can really replace Jensen, I mean, he does the roles of several people,” Musk said Wednesday during an appearance at The New York Times DealBook Summit . “He has long-term relationships that have been built up over decades, he understands the technology incredibly well. His team loves him.”

“You need to think long and hard before kicking someone like that out … he’s certainly made some mistakes,” he added. “I think it’s like kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak, and it just doesn’t seem like a good thing for shareholders.”

Huang’s resignation was announced last week following accusations stemming from a New York Times report in October that claimed American authorities discovered a Chinese businessperson illegally smuggled AI chips into China while developing a “close relationship” with Huang.

The resignation came a day after the Times reported that Huang had a separate affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him, citing five people who worked at the company.

Musk has continued to support the former Nvidia CEO in the past week.

Last week, in a post on social platform X , Musk wrote that without Huang, Nvidia will lose “ critical deals ” noting, “Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract.”

Prior to Huang’s resignation, Musk said it “would be an honor” to hire him, in response to a post on X. He also signed on to a letter calling on Nvidia’s board of directors to reinstate Huang.

“We write with gratitude for Jensen Huang and with a clear demand to the Board: bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts, unless and until you can provide compelling evidence that his removal is in NVIDIA’s best interests,” the letter read.

articles.title: Data center fight snarls amendment votes on energy bill
articles.summary: A Democratic senator says Republicans are blocking his amendment to ban data centers on public lands as amendment votes on a major permitting reform bill sit in limbo. In response to a post from a reporter saying that Oregon Sens. Jeff Merkley (D) and Ron Wyden (D) are holding up votes on amendments to the…
articles.body:
A Democratic senator says Republicans are blocking his amendment to ban data centers on public lands as amendment votes on a major permitting reform bill sit in limbo.

In response to a post from a reporter saying that Oregon Sens. Jeff Merkley (D) and Ron Wyden (D) are holding up votes on amendments to the sweeping energy bill, Wyden said that Republicans are blocking his bid to push an amendment that would ban data centers on public lands.

“Republicans are blocking a simple vote on my amendment to ban data centers on public lands. Republicans are too afraid to stand up to Trump even though Americans overwhelmingly voted to rein in data centers,” Wyden wrote on the social platform X .

Wyden spokesperson Emily Zahnle-Hostetler said in an email that the senator “did not agree to the amendment package because the sponsors won’t allow the promised amendment process that would allow a vote on his data center amendment.”

Merkley’s office confirmed that he, too, is holding up the votes.

The Senate on Wednesday teed up its final passage of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), allowing for 30 hours of consideration in the interim.

A GOP aide told The Hill that senators had been working in good faith to develop a bipartisan list of amendments that could be voted on in the remaining hours, but added that two Democrats were holding up the process. The aide said that the lawmakers could be preventing their colleagues from getting votes on measures that are important to them.

A second GOP aide noted that Wyden opposes the bill and said that the senator is simply trying to slow passage of a bill he does not like.

The BAAJA more broadly seeks to speed up the nation’s ability to build energy and other infrastructure, including things such as power lines, pipelines and more, in part by reining in the nation’s environmental laws.

Its supporters say it will both bring down costs and mitigate climate change with wins for renewable power, while opponents warn of environmental consequences of more fossil fuels and fewer guardrails.

“Data centers are permitted under state and local law. BAAJA does nothing to change that. It does not authorize a single data center on public lands or anywhere else, and Senator Wyden knows it,” said a spokesperson for Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah). “BAAJA actually makes data centers pay more to interconnect to the grid to ensure other customers’ rates don’t increase. This is the same lazy, copy-and-paste argument opponents trot out whenever Congress tries to build something in America.”

It’s not entirely clear what will be voted on during the bill’s amendment process, though many lawmakers have sought changes to the bill’s historic preservation act provisions amid concerns from tribal leaders that the legislation dramatically weakens their ability to weigh in on projects that might impact them. It’s also not clear whether an amendment to change those provisions would actually get the votes they need to pass.

Wyden’s data center amendment comes after reports that the Trump administration was weighing proposals to build data centers on public lands.
