articles.title: JPMorgan Chase reveals data breach, but says it’s unrelated to this week’s banking outage
articles.summary: JPMorgan Chase has confirmed that its third-party vendors have suffered a cyberattack, potentially exposing the names and emails belonging to some of its customers.
articles.body: JPMorgan Chase says its third-party vendors suffered a cyberattack, exposing marketing data like customer names and email addresses. The confirmation follows a report from Cybernews, which says a ransomware group leaked email addresses belonging to around 16,000 JPMorgan Chase customers. In a post about the attack, JPMorgan Chase says “there is no connection” to the outage that occurred earlier this week, which the company attributed to a “software bug:” > We have learned that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack. Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses. > There is no disruption to our services. Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring. There is no connection to service disruption some customers experienced earlier this week. As reported by Cybernews, the leaked dataset appears to include information linked to JPMorgan Chase’s invitation-only Reserve program. The hacking group claiming responsibility for the breach says it targeted Visa and Mastercard as well, both of which confirmed attacks on a third-party vendor, Cybernews reports. “There is no indication that payment data such as card numbers have been affected,” Visa says in a statement to Cybernews. Meanwhile, Mastercard spokesperson Seth Eisen tells The Verge that the breach exposed “a limited amount of email addresses” belonging to a “small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program.” Cybernews says it uncovered datasets connected to 6,000 premium Visa customers, as well as around 2,000 Mastercard customers, if authentic. Update, November 19th: Added information about a Mastercard breach.

articles.title: Mark Ein signs 60-year deal with Trump admin to revamp Rock Creek Tennis Center
articles.summary: Sports business entrepreneur Mark Ein is behind a multimillion-dollar plan to renovate Rock Creek Tennis Center in northwest Washington, D.C., home of the Mubadala DC Open. The $25 million project, announced on Thursday, includes a 60-year lease between Ein’s firm and the Department of Interior that will cover a major overhaul of the property including…
articles.body:
Sports business entrepreneur Mark Ein is behind a multimillion-dollar plan to renovate Rock Creek Tennis Center in northwest Washington, D.C., home of the Mubadala DC Open.

The $25 million project, announced on Thursday , includes a 60-year lease between Ein’s firm and the Department of Interior that will cover a major overhaul of the property including new courts, soccer fields and other amenities.

The deal includes an initial investment of almost $10 million from the District of Columbia government and will entail the rebuilding of the tennis courts from the ground up, upgrading aging court lighting, and sandblasting, painting and making repairs to the rusted and deteriorated stadium.

Renovations will also be made to the public restrooms, food and beverage facilities, support spaces, HVAC and other critical building systems and locker rooms, which will be made available to the public for the first time.

“Our goal is to make the Rock Creek Tennis Center one of the very best public urban tennis and recreation facilities in America and deliver something extraordinary for the District and our region,” Ein said in a statement on Thursday.

“We are going to make the investments that this historic facility has needed for decades, create more opportunities for people to play tennis and other sports year-round, and ensure one of the world’s great professional tennis tournaments stays in Washington, DC.”

Ein is a venture capitalist and D.C. native who has a minority stake in the Washington Commanders, English football club Leeds United and the MLB’s Baltimore Orioles.

Rock Creek is home to the Mubadala DC Open, which is the world’s only combined ATP 500 and WTA 500 professional tennis tournament and brings some of the world’s best men’s and women’s players to the nation’s capital.

articles.title: Microsoft is killing its great tasks app in favor of its worse tasks app
articles.summary: Microsoft To Do will shut down in June 2027, and while business users will be moved to Planner, personal Microsoft users have nowhere to go.
articles.body: In 2015 Microsoft acquired a to-do list app called Wunderlist, for a price rumored to be as high as $200 million. Wunderlist fans were worried that Microsoft would make their beloved app soulless and corporate, or worse, hide it behind some convoluted enterprise subscription. But against all odds, Microsoft was a good steward: The app became Microsoft To Do, but it remained a useful and powerful way for people to manage their tasks across all platforms. Now Microsoft is pulling the rug. Buried deep in a blog post about “unified tasks and plans for Copilot and Microsoft 365” is the news that the To Do apps will “retire” on June 30th, 2027. The transition will be painful: Starting next summer, business users will need to use the Planner app for their tasks, but Microsoft won’t migrate their tasks automatically. And personal users, well, don’t let the door hit you. “Customers using personal Microsoft accounts will need to choose another app,” the blog post reads. From a certain strategic standpoint, you can almost see how this makes sense. (Microsoft hasn’t responded to a request for comment.) It’s definitely true that Microsoft’s task- and project-management offerings are too complicated; To Do and Planner have some overlapping features, and you can use a half-dozen different Microsoft apps to manage your daily tasks. Microsoft has been hinting at bringing everything under the Planner banner for some time, and as Microsoft tries to foist Copilot upon everything you do at work, bringing all that stuff into one place makes more sense. (“More sense” may be relative, though. When your blog post contains sentences like, “Additionally, this unified platform makes accessing Planner through Copilot, Cowork and Autopilot easier because it’s all part of Work IQ,” you still have some work to do.) [Media: It’s also yet another sign that Microsoft is simply giving up on the idea of making software that people use outside of work. Planner isn’t available through a personal or family Microsoft 365 account, so you can’t switch if you want to. Not that you necessarily would: Lots of people liked To Do specifically because it was a list of tasks, not a project management platform. Planner is a business tool for business users, administered by IT professionals and monitored by big bosses. Planner is also, in many ways, just not as good a platform. It doesn’t have a dedicated desktop app — you’re meant to use it on the web, or through Teams or Outlook — and is missing some of To Do’s useful syncing and sharing features. Microsoft is not promising to spend the next six months closing those gaps, or even offering to help people export their data and move on. The company is simply getting all the way out of the business of helping regular people manage their days, and leaving users in the lurch. If you’re suddenly shopping for a new to-do list, the good news is there are plenty of good options. Todoist and TickTick are the two stalwarts of the space, and they offer much of the same ubiquity and simplicity as To Do (though I agree with all the commenters on Reddit and Microsoft’s blog, who say To Do’s interface was better than either one.) Google Tasks is being integrated across Google’s own office suite. The vibe coding revolution has also persuaded approximately every person on the internet to build their own to-do app, so you have lots to choose from. At this point, there’s seemingly only one company left that doesn’t want you managing your days and tasks in its systems, and it’s Microsoft.

articles.title: Hegseth hands Colombia C-130 military transport aircraft
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth formally delivered a Lockheed C-130 Hercules military transport aircraft to Colombia on Wednesday as the Trump administration deepens its defense partnership with the Latin American country. “Like our communities, your communities are threatened by gangs and violence and drugs and narco-terrorism, and you want safe streets and a prosperous country for…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth formally delivered a Lockheed C-130 Hercules military transport aircraft to Colombia on Wednesday as the Trump administration deepens its defense partnership with the Latin American country.

“Like our communities, your communities are threatened by gangs and violence and drugs and narco-terrorism, and you want safe streets and a prosperous country for you and your family. We want that for you too. And this C-130 is a demonstration of our commitment to Colombia,” Hegseth said in a video released by the Pentagon on Thursday.

During Hegseth’s visit to Colombia on Wednesday, he met with Colombian Defense Minister Jorge Mora and Foreign Affairs Minister Omar Bula Escobar in Bogotá, commending the nation for its leadership in the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (A3C), which it joined in August, and its “commitment to countering transnational narco-terrorist organizations.”

The Pentagon said it had nothing more to provide about the trip.

Hours earlier, the Defense secretary was in Venezuela, where he met with acting President Delcy Rodríguez in Caracas, signing a military partnership with the country to help counter foreign actors and “narco-terrorists.”

Since launching the A3C, the Pentagon has looked to partner with the coalition members to conduct joint military operations against alleged drug traffickers and transnational drug cartels.

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, an ally of President Trump, has been a willing partner as the country has one of the most advanced militaries on the continent.

Bula, Colombia’s foreign minister, pressed the nation’s Congress on Wednesday, after the meeting with Hegseth, to greenlight stepped-up military cooperation with the U.S. in its continued fight against drug trafficking.

The U.S. and Colombian forces also recently completed a major military training exercise, called “Southern Vanguard,” that brought together about 350 U.S. military personnel and over 400 Colombian Army soldiers.

“So I’m proud today to sign this particular aircraft, but it’s a symbol of more, symbol of more capabilities, and the fight that we are determined to take, that we will take shoulder to shoulder to the cartels that threaten your country and that threaten our country,” Hegseth said in the video.

In late August, U.S. Southern Command’s head, Marine four-star Gen. Francis Donovan, met with Mora , a port city located in the southwest corner of Colombia.

articles.title: Frontier Airlines launches $399 unlimited flight pass with no blackout dates
articles.summary: Frontier Airlines launched its 2027 GoWild Annual Pass, which offers unlimited flights with no blackout dates at a promotional price starting at $399.
articles.body:
DENVER ( KDVR ) — Frontier Airlines is offering travelers a new way to fly with the launch of its 2027 GoWild Annual Pass, featuring unlimited flights and no blackout dates.

The Denver-based airline announced Wednesday that the pass is available for $399 for a limited time. Discount Den members can purchase it for $349.

According to Frontier, travelers can begin using the pass immediately after purchase and continue flying through Dec. 31, 2027.

For the first time, the GoWild Pass will have no blackout dates, allowing customers to travel during peak periods. However, additional fees may apply.

Passholders can book domestic flights beginning one day before departure and international flights 10 days before departure. Early booking options are also available for additional charges.

While the pass offers unlimited flights, travelers must pay 1 cent in airfare per flight segment, plus applicable taxes and fees. Baggage and seat selections are not included.

Flights and seats are subject to availability.

The airline said reservations are currently open through Aug. 16, 2027, giving travelers an opportunity to plan trips months in advance.

Customers can purchase the pass through Frontier Airlines’ website . The pass automatically renews unless canceled.

articles.title: 148 aboard Florida-bound cruise ship sickened by ‘unknown’ GI outbreak: CDC
articles.summary: Nearly 150 people aboard a Princess cruise ship have been sickened by an “unknown” gastrointestinal illness outbreak, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
articles.body:
FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla. ( WFLA ) — Nearly 150 people aboard a cruise ship have been sickened by an “unknown” gastrointestinal illness outbreak, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

The outbreak was first reported on the Caribbean Princess ship on Sunday, Nov. 15. The ship departed from Fort Lauderdale on Nov. 11.

The CDC said 134 passengers and 14 crew members have reported symptoms.

More than 4,000 passengers and crew members are on board the ship.

The CDC said Princess Cruises and the crew aboard the ship have increased cleaning and disinfection procedures, isolated ill passengers and crew and collected stool specimens from gastrointestinal illness cases for testing.

“Norovirus is often a cause of gastrointestinal illness outbreaks on cruise ships, but we don’t always know the cause of the outbreak when we begin an investigation,” the CDC said. “Finding the agent that caused an outbreak (causative agent) can take time.”

“When an outbreak occurs, people whose symptoms met the case definition are asked to provide stool or vomitus samples,” the health agency continued. “These samples are tested to determine the causative agent.”

Princess Cruises confirmed the news in a statement, saying a “limited” number of passengers were affected.

“Our crew responded promptly by implementing enhanced sanitation protocols across the ship, including comprehensive cleaning and disinfection measures,” the company wrote. “While most guests remain unaffected, we are continuing to closely monitor the situation.”

According to CruiseMapper, the voyage includes five stops and a trip through the Panama Canal. It is set to return to Fort Lauderdale on Monday, Nov. 23.

The Regal Princess and another cruise ship Caribbean Princess that left from Fort Lauderdale have been issued “no sail” orders by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention after crew members who had possibly been exposed on a California ship were tested. The Regal Princess has since docked at the port, and passengers have been able to leave the ship. (AP Photo/Wilfredo Lee)

articles.title: Amazon is pushing alerts opposing NYC’s Delivery Protection Act
articles.summary: Right next to Black Friday ads, Amazon is claiming that NYC’s Delivery Protection Act could add $5 per order.
articles.body: Amazon is serving up push notifications and banners on its home page to some users, warning that a new bill could add up to $5 per order in New York City. The Delivery Protection Act, which is backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani and a number of labor groups, including the Teamsters, would require Amazon to employ its current fleet of third-party delivery contractors directly. Currently, Amazon turns to a network of small delivery companies that often work exclusively with the retailer. This is why your packages are dropped off by a guy in a Toyota Camry sometimes, rather than an Amazon truck. The new bill would require that last-mile delivery firms be licensed by the city and directly employed, rather than operate as contractors. Next to Black Friday deal offers, now Amazon is showing a big tile with a red banner that says, “Attention NYC Council could add up to $5 per order.” Other users are reporting similar notices in the mobile app and after completing orders. In a statement posted to its site, Amazon says that: > If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them [third-party delivery contractors], and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city. That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees. Mayor Mandani and labor unions have countered that the current subcontractor model allows corporations like Amazon to avoid accountability and exploit vulnerable workers. In a statement to The Verge City Council Speaker Julie Menin said: > “It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections. We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs. If Amazon thinks this deceptive campaign will effectively threaten New Yorkers and intimidate this City Council, they are dead wrong.” Amazon’s threats to leave New York to avoid regulation and efforts to unionize within the city follows shortly after the company’s third-quarter earnings report in which it said that it was on its way to having not one, but two trillion-dollar businesses in the next five to ten years. Update November 19th: Added comment from Council Speaker Menin.

articles.title: Oh, Elon Musk is ‘moderate’ now, is he?
articles.summary: After spending nearly half a billion dollars to thwart Democrats, Musk tries to distance himself from MAGA.
articles.body: A little less than two years ago, Elon Musk stood onstage at the Conservative Political Action Conference, sunglasses on, black MAGA hat perched atop his head, wielding a chainsaw. Last night, Musk called in to The New York Times DealBook Summit and distanced himself from President Donald Trump’s movement. “I think I’m ideologically quite moderate. I don’t think I have any kind of extreme political views,” Musk told DealBook editor Andrew Ross Sorkin. “You’ve known me for a long time. Can you think of an extreme view that I have?” I can certainly think of a few. Let’s start with the great replacement. For those who are blissfully unaware, the great replacement is a white nationalist conspiracy theory whose adherents believe that a cabal of powerful people is conspiring to replace white Americans and Europeans by promoting mass migration from the developing world. (The most hardcore great replacement types believe this is a grand Jewish conspiracy; the more politically palatable Fox News types blame Democrats.) As recently as this year, Musk was promoting the notion that white men would be “slaughtered” if they became a minority in the United States. Musk is X’s most prolific promoter of anti-immigrant conspiracy theories, according to a Bloomberg analysis. At a 2024 campaign rally with Trump, Musk claimed that Democrats want to “take away your right to vote effectively.” His racist fearmongering extends beyond the US. At a rally for Germany’s far-right party last year, Musk encouraged Germans to not lose their national values “in some sort of multiculturalism that dilutes everything.” He encouraged Germans to be proud of their heritage, saying there was “frankly too much of a focus on past guilt and we need to move beyond that.” Musk posted about race nearly every single day in the month of January. “Whites,” he wrote, “are a rapidly dying minority.” It’s a claim he’s made multiple times. “If current trends continue, Whites will go from being a small minority of world population today to virtually extinct!” he said in December 2025. Musk, a birth rate obsessive, is doing his part to keep the white race alive. He has fathered at least 14 children with four different women. In fact, fears of replacement animated Musk’s support for Republicans in the midterm elections, to the tune of nearly half a billion dollars. (At the DealBook Summit, Musk said he now feels “pretty foolish” for throwing so much money at Republican campaigns “and not seeing much for it.”) Musk himself said that if Democrats return to power, they’ll “open the borders and legalize everyone living in America illegally to cement a permanent majority.” You could ignore the dogwhistles and argue he meant a permanent political majority, but that would require you to ignore basically every other thing Musk has said about race, migration, and politics over the past four or so years. In 2024, for example, Musk amplified the viral far-right lie that Haitian immigrants in Springfield, Ohio, were eating people’s pets. “Vote for Kamala if you want this to happen to your neighborhood,” Musk posted on X. [Media: The only thing that rivals Musk’s obsession with white birth rates is his fixation on trans people. Musk has repeatedly asserted that his daughter Vivian Wilson, from whom he is estranged, was “killed by the woke mind virus.” (Wilson, who is very much alive, was reportedly cut off from Musk’s health insurance after coming out as transgender.) Shortly after taking over X, Musk decided that the platform would consider the words “cis” and “cisgender” slurs. After J.K. Rowling equated trans activists’ rhetoric to Hitler’s musings on propaganda, Musk reposted her on X, adding, “Precisely.” Sorkin feebly gestured at Musk’s comments about “some of the things happening in Europe and around immigration that people did think were far or extreme,” to say nothing of his MAGA affiliation. Musk countered that he doesn’t think these things are extreme, and also that he’s “not MAGA.” “I’m not sure what MAGA means,” he continued. An interesting thing for the architect of a key part of the MAGA agenda to say! The dizzying pace of news may make it hard to remember just how much damage Musk did to the federal government — and to the world. The chainsaw Musk brandished onstage at CPAC was meant to represent his now-defunct Department of Government Efficiency, which he unofficially led as a government employee under Trump. Musk’s views weren’t an anomaly in DOGE. Marko Elez, a former DOGE staffer — who followed Musk there from SpaceX — resigned after reporters uncovered an old social media account where he urged the US to repeal the Civil Rights Act and reinstate a “eugenic immigration policy.” Elez was subsequently rehired by the Social Security Administration. Though it was never an actual government department, DOGE gutted the federal workforce, infiltrated the Treasury Department and the Social Security Administration, and dismantled USAID, resulting in hundreds of thousands of deaths around the world. [Media: Shortly after Trump’s return to office, Musk called USAID — which, until he and his DOGE staffers destroyed it, provided people across the developing world with lifesaving food and medical aid — a “criminal organization.” Earlier this year, amid mass opposition to ICE’s Operation Metro Surge in Minneapolis — during which federal agents killed two US citizens — Musk defended DHS against its critics. “It is pure evil for people to stop the arrest of child predators,” he wrote on X. Musk is a creature of the internet, and as such he’s left a pretty extensive paper trail of his beliefs. As recently as October, he was endorsing a reposted screenshot of a 4chan post arguing that women shouldn’t participate in democracy because they “can’t defend themselves physically,” saying it “sounds correct.” Charles Cornish-Dale, the pseudonymous X user behind the post, who goes by Raw Egg Nationalist, is a far-right British bodybuilder who edits the magazine Man’s World. Given the on-again, off-again nature of their relationship, it’s surprising that Musk’s comments about MAGA were so well received by Trump. “Oh, I don’t know. He’s a friend of mine. What can I tell you? I mean, you have to ask — there are lots of definitions out there,” Trump told reporters. “MAGA, to me, means something very specific, and when people veer from it, they don’t do very well. But Elon is — Elon’s got very good intentions. I mean, he was with me the whole — he traveled with me.” The public has broadly rejected the chaos wrought by MAGA 2.0, and Musk is trying to distance himself from the fallout. More cynically, he’s probably also trying to prevent Democrats in Congress and in Texas from investigating him come 2027. Whatever his motivation, Musk knows the winds have shifted, though his pivot is even less convincing than Alex Karp’s. Though, to be fair, there is earlier video evidence of Musk saying he isn’t MAGA. “I’m not just MAGA,” he said at a 2024 Trump rally in Madison Square Garden. “I’m dark, gothic MAGA.” Update, November 19th: This post has been updated to include Trump’s response to Musk’s comments.

articles.title: Anthropic opens at $111.50 per share after largest IPO ever
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic opened at $111.50 per share Wednesday, after the company wrapped up the largest initial public offering (IPO) on record. Anthropic, which is trading under the ticker “ANT,” and certain stockholders sold 980 million shares of the company’s stock valued at $83 per share, the AI firm announced Wednesday. That brought the…
articles.body:
Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic opened at $111.50 per share Wednesday, after the company wrapped up the largest initial public offering (IPO) on record.

Anthropic, which is trading under the ticker “ANT,” and certain stockholders sold 980 million shares of the company’s stock valued at $83 per share, the AI firm announced Wednesday .

That brought the company’s IPO to more than $81.3 billion, the largest in history. Anthropic had aimed to raise more than $64 billion at a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion for its IPO, based on the company’s most recent filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The Claude maker is the first pure play AI lab to go public, beating competitors such as OpenAI less than six years after co-founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei departed the latter company and founded Anthropic.

Anthropic’s stock dipped below $100 per share within 30 minutes of its Nasdaq composite debut and was trading at roughly $96.60 per share as of the early afternoon.

Elon Musk’s SpaceX set the previous IPO record in June, raising $75 billion as it went public at $150 per share. The firm, whose stock market debut made Musk the world’s first trillionaire , sold an additional $11 billion worth of shares after its underwriters exercised their option to purchase the maximum amount of shares.

SpaceX’s stock has fluctuated over the last five months and is trading at below $138 per share as of Thursday afternoon.

Anthropic going public coincides with a rocky couple of weeks for the AI industry, as Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia sent shockwaves through the company responsible for powering the technology via its chips .

Lawmakers on Capitol Hill have also sounded the alarm bells about Anthropic’s IPO, as Americans express concerns about AI’s impact on the labor market and its implications for humanity .

“The pressure to deliver profits will be immediate, and it will be immense,” Rep. Pat Ryan (D-N.Y.) wrote Wednesday on the social platform X, referring to Anthropic.

“I’m not writing this because I doubt the technology is powerful,” he added . “I’m writing this because I’m terrified of the choices Anthropic will make to justify their valuation.”

articles.title: Pentagon has no department-wide plan to address munitions shortages, watchdog report finds
articles.summary: Despite a munitions shortfall exacerbated by the Trump administration’s war in Iran, the Pentagon does not have a department-wide plan to address the issue long-term, a federal watchdog said in a new report released Thursday. The Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that while the Defense Department has taken steps toward increasing its munitions inventory, it…
articles.body:
Despite a munitions shortfall exacerbated by the Trump administration’s war in Iran, the Pentagon does not have a department-wide plan to address the issue long-term, a federal watchdog said in a new report released Thursday.

The Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that while the Defense Department has taken steps toward increasing its munitions inventory, it “doesn’t have an overarching plan that identifies long-term goals, strategies, or ways to measure its progress.”

As part of the problem, the Pentagon does not have a dedicated office with authority to improve munition inventories, making it harder for the department “to know whether its munitions production efforts are really addressing department-wide needs.”

The status of U.S. munitions reserves remains murky at best, but what is known is that Washington blew through a significant portion of its long-range cruise missiles and interceptors in the beginning of the Iran war, which began on Feb. 28.

In March, for example, it was reported that U.S. forces burned through at least 850 Tomahawk missiles in the first month of the conflict known as Operation Epic Fury. It’s estimated the Pentagon has just a few thousand left.

And in August, Reuters reported the Army had used up “virtually all” of its global stockpile of long-range missiles such as the Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS) and Precision Strike Missiles.

While top administration officials have insisted the U.S. military has the weapons needed for an intense military offensive against Iran should fighting resume, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao on Tuesday revealed this week that his service recoded and fired missiles he described as “expired.”

“A lot of the munitions we used in Epic Fury, we were able to recode those,” Cao said during a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing on his nomination to become Navy secretary.

“They were code echo, code foxtrot, which means they’re expired. But, you know, I came from a poor family, right? Things like bread doesn’t expire. You just rub some water on it, microwave it for 15 seconds and it’s good to go,” he said.

Reports also have suggested that weapons shortages are a factor in persuading President Trump to hold back on escalating attacks against Iran.

“A key part of military readiness is having a reliable supply of munitions, including bombs, missiles, and torpedoes. But the Department of Defense has faced persistent munitions shortages,” the GAO wrote in a summary of its new report. “The 2026 conflict with Iran only reinforced the challenges with the munitions inventory.”

“DOD [Department of Defense] has taken steps toward increasing its inventory, but could do more,” the watchdog adds, noting that in lieu of a plan, the Pentagon and the military services “can be reactive to global events rather than driven by total requirements.”

And while the Defense Department has a department-wide munitions data tool to track munitions, the GAO found that it has limited oversight over this instrument and has not regularly conducted inventory check ins with the services.

The watchdog recommended that the Pentagon come up with an overarching plan to improve inventory levels that links building munitions and funding to department requirements and include long-term goals, strategies to achieve them and ways to gauge progress.

In addition, it suggests the Defense secretary identify an office to implement the munitions plan and set regular timelines to check munitions inventories.

The Hill reached out to the Pentagon for comment on the report.

articles.summary: A single data broker opt-out may not be enough. Spokeo, Whitepages and BeenVerified can still expose your address and family details to scammers.
articles.body: Many retirees think they're protecting their privacy by staying off social media, removing their information from one people-search site or paying for credit monitoring. But a single data broker opt-out request may leave your home address, phone number and family details exposed elsewhere. With the holidays approaching, now is a good time to find out what's available about you online and take steps to remove it. People-search sites like Spokeo, Whitepages and BeenVerified can make personal details available to strangers. Some information is free to view, while more detailed reports may require payment. And here's where it gets concerning. A scammer who knows your grandson's name or where your daughter lives could use those details to make a fake emergency call sound convincing. WHY CAREFUL PEOPLE STILL END UP ON DATA BROKER SITES Where your personal information comes from You don't need a social media account to have your information collected. Data brokers gather information from public records, including property deeds, voter registration records where accessible and court filings. They may also obtain details from commercial databases, online activity and companies that collect personal information. Over time, those details can become part of a profile showing where you live, previous addresses, phone numbers and possible family connections. According to the Federal Trade Commission, opting out of one people-search site doesn't remove your information from others. Your details may also reappear when public records change or websites collect updated information. For older adults, the financial risks can be especially serious. An FTC report released in October 2026 found that adults ages 60 and older reported approximately $3 billion in fraud losses during 2025. Although older adults reported losing money to fraud less frequently than younger adults overall, their reported individual losses tended to be higher. You can use a free exposure scanner at CyberGuy.com to check whether your personal information appears on publicly searchable websites. The data broker opt-out steps to take now You can start removing your personal information yourself without paying for a service. A credit freeze won't remove your information from data brokers, and credit monitoring generally alerts you to possible problems rather than preventing your details from appearing online. These tools serve different purposes. One thing to remember: Removing your information from people-search sites doesn't erase public records. Your details may still appear in property records, court documents or even listings connected to family members. That's why it's important to check more than your own name. Doing this yourself can take hours, especially when you're dealing with multiple websites. And because data brokers continue collecting information, the work may need to be repeated. DATA BROKER OPT-OUT: HOW RETIREES CAN PROTECT THEIR DATA Free tools that can help remove your information Before paying for a data removal service, there are two other options worth knowing about. Google's Results about you Google offers a free tool called Results about you that can help you find personal information appearing in Google Search. Depending on eligibility, you may be able to request the removal of results containing your home address, phone number or email address. Here's how to get started: Keep in mind that removing a Google search result doesn't delete the information from the original website. You may still need to contact the site directly. California's free DROP privacy service If you live in California, you have another option. The state's free Delete Request and Opt-out Platform, called DROP, launched in January 2026. It allows eligible California residents to submit a single deletion request covering more than 600 registered data brokers. Beginning Aug. 1, 2026, covered data brokers were required to start processing requests through the system. Removal can take time, and some information may be exempt under the law. You can submit a request and check its status at California's official DROP website at privacy.ca.gov/drop/. Other states also have privacy laws that may give residents additional rights to request deletion of their information. WHY REMOVING YOUR DATA ONLINE MAY STILL LEAVE YOUR FAMILY EXPOSED How a personal data removal service can help If you don't want to spend hours contacting websites and tracking removal requests, a personal data removal service can help. These services contact data brokers on your behalf and submit requests to remove your personal information. Depending on the provider and plan, features may include: Some services offer ongoing monitoring and follow-up requests, which can save time compared with handling each website yourself. It's important to understand that no service can guarantee every piece of personal information will disappear from the internet. Public records may remain accessible, and some websites may fall outside the service's coverage. Still, reducing the number of places where your information appears can make your personal details harder to find. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com. Bring this conversation to the Thanksgiving table Thanksgiving brings families together, making it a great opportunity to talk about protecting everyone's personal information. You don't need to make it a lengthy discussion. A few simple checks can help everyone understand what scammers may already know about them. 1) Check what's online about your family After dinner, sit down with a family member and search your names on a few people-search sites. Look for home addresses, phone numbers and family connections. If you find something you don't want publicly available, discuss how to request its removal. Check your parents' information, too, with their permission. Even if you've removed your own details, your name or address may still appear in a relative's profile. 2) Agree on a family code word Choose a private phrase that family members can use if someone calls claiming there's an emergency. Avoid birthdays, pet names or other details someone could easily discover online. Agree on the phrase privately rather than sharing it in a group chat. A code word adds another layer of protection, but it shouldn't be your only way to verify someone's identity. 3) Verify unexpected emergency calls If someone claims to be a grandchild or another relative who urgently needs money, don't send anything until you've checked the story. Hang up and call your loved one directly using a phone number you already know. If you can't reach them, contact another trusted family member. Scammers can now use AI voice cloning to sound like someone you love. That means even a familiar voice may not be enough to prove who's calling. Learn more about how AI voice scams can clone your family's voice and what you can do to protect yourself. And be especially suspicious if someone demands payment through gift cards, cryptocurrency or wire transfers. 4) Make a family plan before someone calls Agree that nobody will send emergency money based solely on an unexpected phone call or text. If something sounds suspicious, contact another family member before taking action. Scammers often pressure people to respond immediately or keep the situation secret. The more your family talks about these tactics ahead of time, the easier it becomes to recognize a suspicious request. Scammers may already know more about your family than you realize. A private code word adds protection, but always confirm an unexpected emergency by contacting your loved one directly before sending money. Kurt's key takeaways Here's what concerns me. Removing that information once is a good start, but it can show up again. That's why I recommend checking these sites regularly or using a trusted data removal service to help handle the work. articles.title: O’Reilly suggests building technology like Iron Dome to prevent hackers: ‘They’re not going away’
articles.summary: Conservative commentator Bill O’Reilly said there should be a bipartisan effort to develop technology like the Iron Dome to protect the U.S.’s technology infrastructure against hackers. “Both parties are going to have to say, look, we have to develop technology just as we did with the Iron Dome and the space weaponry, all that, to…
articles.body:
Conservative commentator Bill O’Reilly said there should be a bipartisan effort to develop technology like the Iron Dome to protect the U.S.’s technology infrastructure against hackers.

“Both parties are going to have to say, look, we have to develop technology just as we did with the Iron Dome and the space weaponry, all that, to protect our infrastructure from hackers, because they’re not going away,” O’Reilly said during an appearance on NewsNation’s “Katie Pavlich Tonight.”

O’Reilly’s suggestion comes as Americans are recovering from widespread technology outages in the past week that have impacted flights, banking systems and more.

On Nov. 12, Microsoft faced global outages that impacted its platforms Outlook and Teams. The incident, which lasted about a day, was “introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” the company said.

A day later, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop that lasted more than four hours. Authorities attributed the incident to an overload of data on routers. Thousands of flights were delayed and canceled on Friday, impacting operations through the weekend.

Customers of several banks including Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo had trouble accessing their accounts Monday. A spokesperson from JPMorgan Chase told The Hill the cause was “a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems” and denied anything “cyber-related.”

Speculations flared over whether the outages were linked to a cyberattack, but Trump administration officials, including Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, have repeatedly said that is not the case.

In a Fox News interview , Mullin noted that he could say with “98 percent certainty” that the outages were not linked to a cyberattack but said “SI” or super intelligence could have been the reason.

Chase said Thursday on the social platform X that “third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack.”

“Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses,” the company added.

Raising concerns over hackers during the NewsNation interview, O’Reilly said, “There are millions of them. And they’re mercenaries. They’re criminals. They’re awful. And they can destroy lives. They can destroy countries.”

On Tuesday, the National Security Agency (NSA) faced a network outage , which disrupted the operations of NSANet, a classified internal network used by employees.

“They got into the NSA stuff today,” O’Reilly said. “The hackers got in. Now, don’t tell me that’s a functional thing. It’s not. These are targeted things.”

O’Reilly emphasized that when President Trump returns from his trip to China , where he took part in a rare three-way talk with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, “he has to bring in all his tech people and security people and figure this out.”

articles.title: FCC greenlights rule allowing prisons to jam cellphone signals
articles.summary: The FCC has voted to pass a rule allowing state and local prisons to jam cellphones. The agency argues the rule will help combat an “influx of contraband cellphones” used to carry out crimes from prison.
articles.body: The Federal Communications Commission voted unanimously to allow state and local prisons to jam cellphones. In an announcement on Thursday, the FCC argues the rule will help combat an “influx of contraband cellphones” used to carry out crimes from prison. Jammers are generally banned under Section 333 of the Communications Act of 1934, though they’re used at some federal facilities. FCC Chair Brendan Carr claims that giving correctional facilities access to this technology will help prevent prisoners from using phones for illegal activity. “These devices [phones] are being used by inmates to order hits, run drug operations, traffic women and children, and unleash mayhem on our communities from behind bars,” Carr says. In the months leading up to the vote, trade groups and human rights advocates have raised concerns about the risks of blocking cellphone signals in prisons. The US Chamber of Commerce and the CTIA, a wireless association representing the nation’s biggest carriers, have both warned in letters to the FCC that jamming technology could disrupt lawful communications outside prisons, including 911 calls. Meanwhile, the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) has long argued that cellphones can keep prisoners safe by allowing them to document safety and human rights issues that the outside world may not see. FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, the sole Democrat on the Commission, voted for the measure despite the risk of “potential unintended consequences,” according to the Associated Press. “I want to make sure that we don’t harm public safety in the name of helping public safety,” Gomez added. The FCC says prisons that choose to jam cellphone signals will need to obtain a license, adhere to “technical standards and testing requirements,” and ensure that the jamming technology doesn’t interfere with communications outside the facility. Prisons must also notify nearby communities of testing and when the technology is being deployed.

articles.title: Baltimore Mayor blasts Marlon Humphrey after Raven’s ‘criminals’ comment
articles.summary: The mayor of Baltimore blasted Ravens cornerback Marlon Humphrey for comments the defensive back made on a podcast earlier this week disparaging the city. Humphrey was asked during a recent episode of his podcast what Baltimore “is the best at making.” “Criminals,” he responded before bursting out into laughter. The comment was met with widespread…
articles.body:
The mayor of Baltimore blasted Ravens cornerback Marlon Humphrey for comments the defensive back made on a podcast earlier this week disparaging the city.

Humphrey was asked during a recent episode of his podcast what Baltimore “is the best at making.”

“Criminals,” he responded before bursting out into laughter.

The comment was met with widespread condemnation online and earned him a rebuke from his team, which sent Humphrey home from the team’s trip to North Carolina to take on the Panthers this weekend.

The defensive back apologized for the comment after practice according to ESPN on Wednesday saying “as you guys know, I’ve been here my whole career. Spent lots of offseasons here. Welcomed a son here and I’m an investor in the city. And obviously, I do know the effect that words have and just like to apologize for those comments.”

Baltimore’s mayor Brandon Scott (D) was not satisfied.

“While we acknowledge Marlon’s apology, a verbal apology is not enough,” Scott said. “Baltimore is a city full of young Black boys who look to the Ravens as a beacon of light in their lives and to have someone that looks like them who wears a Baltimore Ravens jersey relegate them to becoming criminals cuts deeper.”

He added, “I wonder how he would feel if prominent Baltimoreans used their platforms to imply that Baltimore once produced great defensive backs, but we have recently lost our way.”

The mayor also noted he was inviting Humphrey “to sit down with me and some Baltimoreans who have re-entered into our community and are now preventing others from making the mistakes they made.”

Humphrey was one of several Ravens who attended a recent trip President Trump made to the Baltimore area before the midterm elections .

The Ravens won four of their first five games this season but lost to the previously winless Los Angeles Chargers on Monday.

articles.title: Cryptocurrency industry stares down new Congress: 5 takeaways from Capitol Crypto Forum
articles.summary: The cryptocurrency industry is facing a political reckoning as Democrats with a more skeptical view of digital assets prepare to take control of Congress, casting uncertainty about the industry’s legislative prospects. As the industry scrambles to make inroads with the incoming majority following the midterms, the uncertain future of crypto policy loomed over The Hill…
articles.body:
The cryptocurrency industry is facing a political reckoning as Democrats with a more skeptical view of digital assets prepare to take control of Congress, casting uncertainty about the industry’s legislative prospects.

As the industry scrambles to make inroads with the incoming majority following the midterms, the uncertain future of crypto policy loomed over The Hill and The Block’s “ Capitol Crypto Forum ” on Thursday, where lawmakers and industry leaders were divided over the prospects for reviving stalled legislation.

The crypto world had a powerful ally in President Trump and a GOP-controlled Congress after a series of clashes with Biden-era regulators. Trump-appointed regulators eased federal oversight of digital assets, numerous investigations were dropped against digital asset firms and Republicans passed landmark legislation establishing the first regulatory framework for stablecoins.

But after the Clarity Act, a major crypto regulation bill , failed to pass the Senate, insiders agree that the chances to revive the effort are slim. Now, the industry is bracing for what’s next from the newly Democratic-controlled committees and crypto’s future in Washington.

Here are five takeaways from Thursday’s event, which was sponsored by Bitget, Latham & Watkins and Block, Inc.

Rep. French Hill (R-Ark.), chair of the House Financial Services Committee, pointed to the 78 Democrats who backed the Clarity Act in the House as evidence that the industry still has allies across the aisle.

“We had a lot of support from Democrats, both on the House and Agriculture Committee and the House Financial Services Committee, and I expect that’ll continue in the new Congress,” Hill said.

Hill said he was encouraged by a memorandum from Rep. Maxine Waters (D-Calif.), who is hoping to succeed him as chair, outlining digital asset market structure as an issue she intends to work on.

Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), a co-sponsor of the Clarity Act, pointed to an unlikely partnership with longtime crypto critic Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) as someone on the Democratic side to help advance crypto legislation.

“I’ll blow all your minds. I’ve had conversations with Elizabeth Warren, where she says, ‘I want the industry regulated. I just don’t want the industry to write the regulations,’” Moreno said, praising Warren for being “very, very smart” and “very thorough.”

Rep. Steven Horsford (D-Nev.) — who is the lead sponsor of the Digital Asset Protection, Accountability, Regulation, Innovation, Taxation and Yields (PARITY) Act — was also optimistic that a bipartisan agreement could be reached but stressed that lawmakers must address concerns about ethics and transparency.

“We do need to get the legislation right,” Horsford said. “I just hope that everyone stays at the table.”

The Clarity Act’s failure to pass the Senate in September left many of its backers questioning whether Congress squandered its best opportunity to pass its most important item in crypto’s legislative agenda.

Hill said he regretted the decision to separate the Clarity Act from the GENIUS Act, the stablecoin legislation signed into law last year, arguing that prolonged negotiations allowed new demands to pile up and made reaching an agreement increasingly difficult.

“I had urged the Senate and the administration last summer to have Clarity [Act] and GENIUS [Act] passed together in the House, and I still stand by that. I think it would have been the right decision,” he said. “I regret that they were separated.”

Stu Alderoty, the chief legal officer at technology company Ripple, acknowledged that the disagreements within the cryptocurrency industry also complicated negotiations, citing disputes over stablecoin rewards and the Trump family’s involvement in crypto “overwhelming the conversation.”

“I think the industry can do a better job of speaking with one voice,” he said.

Regardless, most agreed that with just weeks left for the 119th Congress, the odds were not favorable of a revamped version of the bill passing anytime soon.

Crypto caught in the political crossfire

The crypto industry poured millions into this year’s midterm elections, aggressively throwing their support behind crypto-friendly candidates in more than 100 races across the country.

Despite its heavy spending in the midterms, the industry still faced crushing defeats in key races, including spending $55 million against Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) who defeated incumbent Sen. Jon Husted (R).

At Thursday’s forum, Moreno lamented how cryptocurrency regulation had become entangled in partisan politics.

“The industry should have never gotten sucked into the political vortex,” Moreno said. “This isn’t a Democrat or Republican issue in my mind.”

Peter Van Valkenburgh, the executive director of Coin Center, pointed to another political divide: the Democratic Party’s internal debate over its approach to the emerging technology.

“There’s a battle for the soul of the Democratic Party with respect to tech policy,” Van Valkenburgh said, pointing to the increasing skepticism around artificial intelligence and other forms of advanced technology.

He argued that Democrats who are in favor of technological innovation have struggled to counter the party’s more skeptical and louder voices.

“There’s a very strong anti-tech vision being articulated in parts of the Democratic Party, and the voices for a tech-forward Democratic Party, they haven’t found their song yet,” he said.

Could regulators step in where Congress couldn’t?

With the Clarity Act stalled, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) could take the lead in establishing clearer regulatory rules.

Moreno argued that regulators could accomplish much of what Congress failed to do through formal rulemaking.

But Hill was less convinced, warning that agency regulations could face lawsuits and be reversed by future administrations.

“It’s not a permanent fix,” Hill said. “It’s subject to litigation. It does not have the force of law.”

Kristin Smith, a cryptocurrency industry advocate and interim CEO of Blockchain Association, noted that regulators may be better positioned to tackle the complexities of digital asset policy.

“The learning curve for your average member of Congress or staffer is huge,” she said, pointing to the SEC and CFTC’s expertise in regulating financial markets.

She suggested that allowing agencies to develop rules now could make it easier for Congress to address remaining gaps through more focused legislation in the future.

Prediction markets tout election accuracy

Prediction markets emerged from the midterms with a strong showing , correctly predicting a significant portion of races.

Brian Quintenz, a board member at prediction market platform Kalshi, praised the betting markets’ accuracy in predicting the outcome of the midterm elections, arguing that they provided voters with valuable information as results came in.

“I think the markets did an incredible job,” he said, adding that the results showed prediction markets’ ability to assess polling data and accurately price election results.

The former CFTC commissioner pointed to the Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska, where prediction markets quickly signaled the shock Democratic upsets from Sen.-elect Scott Colom and Sen.-elect Mary Peltola, respectively, as votes began to be counted.

“You had markets providing a very clear signal about what was going to happen, what did happen, in a way that I think actually added credibility and integrity to those outcomes,” he said. “In my mind, a huge success.”

But the industry’s rapid growth has drawn scrutiny from lawmakers concerned about market manipulation and insider trading from those who could profit from their access to crucial information.

articles.title: These tech outages are giving Y2K, AI agent style | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Are the recent outages in the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms really a coincidence? There's actually likely something deeper going on, cybersecurity experts say.
articles.body:
It’s going down, as the American rapper Yung Joc might say: the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms. In the past two weeks, the U.S.’s top businesses have faced technical outages that have disrupted the systems that run everyday life.

Apple Pay went down. NASA’s internal communication network went down. The FAA had to ground all flights for hours (only the third time in history since 9/11), and Microsoft was hit with an outage that took down Outlook, Teams, and Copilot for nearly two days.

The first thought, naturally, is an AI hacker invasion of some sort, especially after hackers managed to attack fridges in a grocery store and a blood bank in France a few weeks ago. Here in the U.S., the director of National Intelligence said these outages don’t seem related to state-sponsored terrorism, while President Trump called the issues “individual events.” Many of the companies themselves have said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks or AI attacks, but tech issues.

Only, there’s the fact that they all struck within a short timespan of each other, and just a few weeks after Cybersecurity’s so-called “Black October,” when a slew of also-unrelated cybersecurity incidents occurred on October 21, striking PHP, Node.js, LiteLLM, more.

While there’s no reason to view these outages as cyberattacks, there may be more than coincidence going on: It’s giving AI-native Y2K, frankly.

Dave DeWalt, an investor who worked in cybersecurity for more than three decades (including as president and CEO of McAfee and as vice chairman of the CISA Advisory Council for the Department of Homeland Security), also thinks it’s probably AI-related.

The technical outages are most likely the “growing pains of a security system that’s getting stronger, not weaker,” and that “AI is surfacing vulnerabilities at a speed and scale we’ve never had before through AI tools like Mythos and others,” he told TechCrunch.

The thing is, many of these technical flaws have always existed, but because AI is surfacing them so fast, enterprises are rushing to fix them before bad actors can exploit them. “That surge in patching is disrupting things in the short term,” he said.

This was, perhaps, the first moment when legacy meets modern, Anusha Iyer, a software engineer and founder of the security startup Corsha, told TechCrunch. “These industrial systems were never designed to be connected, let alone securely connected in the way we are pushing them to be today,” she said.

Virginia Senator Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intel Committee, came to a similar conclusion (although investigations are still underway as to what could be happening). “These disruptions should serve as a wake-up call. It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” the senator wrote on X .

AI is reshaping how software is built, deployed, and operated, on a scale where everyone feels the sharp learning curve. Iyer cited the FAA outage as an example of legacy tech that is not as sophisticated or advanced as the technologies companies are trying to merge it with.

In less technical terms, she said the outage may have been caused (and preliminary findings point to this) when the FAA was trying to modernize its telecommunications infrastructure and the transition overwhelmed parts of its legacy hardware, where the new tech likely operated at a normal modern capacity while the legacy hardware couldn’t keep up.

When looked at this way, she said, AI is actually getting the bad rep. “It’s not rapid adoption of AI yet causing these outages,” she said. “The fault is the rushed mix of the legacy and modern systems without a clear understanding of operational and cyber risk or the ability to gatekeep and protect the legacy systems.”

Organizations need a more steadfast approach to AI adoption, including more testing and prioritizing what needs to be fixed and when, DeWalt said.

Iyer added, “These industrial systems need to be segmented more tightly and more access controlled, so as modern systems are introduced, it can be phased in and risk mitigated.”

Actually, there might be a silver lining to all of this for companies (and for venture investors). DeWalt said he’d rather see these U.S. enterprises find and patch their flaws, even in this messy way, than have bad actors find and exploit those vulnerabilities in AI warfare that could cause even more national security issues.

And maybe some aspiring founders were inspired by them. DeWalt expects a rise in companies focused on “AI-driven vulnerability management, autonomous remediation, safe patch testing and deployment, and resilience for the systems that keep critical infrastructure running,” he said.

“There’s real pain in this transition as we’ve seen in the past week,” DeWalt said. “But there’s also enormous opportunity for the companies that help organizations move at AI speed without breaking things.”

articles.title: Trump administration approved shipment of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China
articles.summary: The Trump administration approved the shipment of nearly 900,000 AI chips to Defense Department-designated Chinese military companies, according to newly released documents from the House Foreign Affairs Committee. The documents revealed the U.S. signed off on the sale of 879,868 AI semiconductor chips from Nvidia and AMD. The specific chips sold were Nvidia’s sensitive H200…
articles.body:
The Trump administration approved the shipment of nearly 900,000 AI chips to Defense Department-designated Chinese military companies, according to newly released documents from the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

The documents revealed the U.S. signed off on the sale of 879,868 AI semiconductor chips from Nvidia and AMD. The specific chips sold were Nvidia’s sensitive H200 chips along with their AMD equivalent.

The order was fulfilled through 21 license applications as of May 11 — including sending 75,000 to Alibaba, 150,000 to Tencent and its subsidiaries, 43,000 to Baidu and 4,000 to BYD. The four companies were all identified on the Defense Department’s 2026 list of alleged Chinese military companies operating in the U.S.

The committee wrote that under the Export Control Reform Act, Rep. Brian Mast (R-Fla.), chair of the panel, was able to “publicly reveal export control license application information” related to Nvidia and AMD’s AI chip licenses for China.

Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), ranking member on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, accused the Trump administration of mishandling chip export controls , saying it “has put our national security and technology edge at risk.”

He also bashed the Bureau of Industry and Security for failing “to enforce the rules,” adding that “Congress must now conduct rigorous oversight of the administration’s policies.”

An Nvidia spokesperson told The Hill, “the review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes.”

“Despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China,” the spokesperson added.

“AMD complies with applicable U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations,” AMD told The Hill in a statement.

Mast has led probes in the House into the Trump administration’s approval of Nvidia’s H200 chips last year. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang previously argued to federal government officials that the sale of its third or fourth best chips would make China dependent on the U.S.-made infrastructure.

articles.title: Trump posthumously pardons Pete Rose
articles.summary: President Trump on Thursday posthumously pardoned famed baseball player Pete Rose, an idea he’s been floating for nearly two years. “I have just given a Complete and Total Pardon to the Late, Great Pete Rose, a true Baseball SUPERSTAR & LEGEND, whose record of 4,256 Hits in a Season will never be broken,” he wrote…
articles.body:
President Trump on Thursday posthumously pardoned famed baseball player Pete Rose, an idea he’s been floating for nearly two years.

“I have just given a Complete and Total Pardon to the Late, Great Pete Rose, a true Baseball SUPERSTAR & LEGEND, whose record of 4,256 Hits in a Season will never be broken,” he wrote on Truth Social.

Trump listed out Rose’s accomplishments and said he was “treated terribly by Major League Baseball in not allowing him to go into the Baseball Hall of Fame.”

He did not say what the pardon was for specifically.

Rose served five months in federal prison for tax evasion. Separately, he was permanently banned from baseball in August 1989 after an investigation found he bet on baseball games, including his own team, the Cincinnati Reds. He never bet against the Reds.

He died in September 2024 at the age of 83.

Trump first mentioned the idea of a pardon in March 2025.

“Major League Baseball didn’t have the courage or decency to put the late, great, Pete Rose, also known as ‘Charlie Hustle,’ into the Baseball Hall of fame,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post at the time.

“Now he is dead, will never experience the thrill of being selected, even though he was a FAR BETTER PLAYER than most of those who made it, and can only be named posthumously. WHAT A SHAME,” he continued.

MLB reinstated Rose last May. It came after Trump had spoken to the commissioner about reinstating Rose.

Trump earlier this month in an impromptu press briefing said, “It’s fair to pardon Pete Rose,” calling the former Cincinnati Reds player “very mistreated.”

“He was gambling. He shouldn’t have done it,” Trump said. “But he went through 40 years of hell, and they never — And they should have given him a pardon. They should have given him into the Baseball Hall of Fame a long time ago.”

articles.title: Exiting GOP senators become liability for Trump
articles.summary: Senate Republicans are set to lose eight members in January, and a few of them are not going easy. These members have become occasional critics of the administration, more willing to hold up President Trump’s agenda or personnel when they see a need for it. The pattern reflects the major loss Trump took in the…
articles.body:
Senate Republicans are set to lose eight members in January, and a few of them are not going easy.

These members have become occasional critics of the administration, more willing to hold up President Trump’s agenda or personnel when they see a need for it.

The pattern reflects the major loss Trump took in the midterm elections, as blind loyalty to the president was generally a vulnerability for Republicans.

Now, some of the Republicans who lost their seats are more open to exercising their power to rebuke Trump choices they see as unwise.

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), who lost his primary in May to Trump-backed Rep. Julia Letlow (R-La.), was among the Republicans on the Senate Health Committee who rejected Jim O’Neill , a science and technology investor and Trump’s nominee to lead the National Science Foundation, on Wednesday.

Cassidy, who has become a fierce critic of Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., said the vote to advance O’Neill had been canceled due a lack of support.

O’Neill “did not do enough to stand up for science and against irresponsible decisions and statements” from Kennedy, Cassidy said. He noted he was not the only committee member who harbored such concerns.

“I like Jim personally, but this time requires leadership and fortitude and standing up for what is right,” Cassidy said.

Prior to O’Neill, Cassidy had voted to advance every Trump health nominee who appeared in front of his committee, overcoming any misgivings.

Cassidy also had concerns about Heidi Overton, Trump’s nominee to lead the Food and Drug Administration, but seemed ready to vote for her anyway until the White House suddenly withdrew her nomination the night before her scheduled hearing.

Cassidy’s relationship with the president has been complicated. The Louisiana senator voted to convict the president in 2021 following the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol attack, but has tried to show he is still loyal, including by casting the deciding vote to confirm Kennedy as HHS secretary.

But since he lost his reelection bid, Cassidy has repeatedly clashed with Kennedy.

In an interview on “Face the Nation” on Sunday, Cassidy called Kennedy’s tenure at HHS “ a series of failures ,” although he stopped short of saying he regretted his vote for the secretary.

Cassidy, as a committee chair, is uniquely positioned to intervene on controversial nominees.

But the structure and traditions of the Senate allow individual senators who want to make a statement to exert significant influence. That could foreshadow more pushback from outgoing Republicans, who have little left to lose, on Trump policies and people.

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) recently used his power as a home-state senator to disapprove of T. Elliot Gaiser, a Trump nominee to be a district judge in Texas.

Cornyn said he opposed Gaiser because he is not from Texas and does not have trial experience.

Cornyn’s office said he had recommended another nominee to the administration months ago.

He then did not submit a “blue slip,” which is essentially a stamp of approval from a senator for judicial nominees in their state.

“I just refuse to be jammed by a non-Texan who has no trial experience, who hasn’t been vetted,” Cornyn told CNN this week. “And so, we provided the White House an alternative, and I’m hoping they take advantage of it because I don’t want the seat to go vacant either.”

Gaiser’s nomination will likely not go forward without Cornyn’s approval.

The move has garnered the outgoing senator plenty of criticism from others on the right, including Heritage Foundation President Kevin Roberts, who lambasted Cornyn online for the move.

“John Cornyn is going out as the Republican Texas Senator who helped get radical leftist James Talarico’s agenda started early. What a legacy,” Roberts wrote on social media Thursday, responding to a news article about the Gaiser nomination.

He earned a sharp reply back from Cornyn: “Kevin, your sycophancy has destroyed the credibility of a once great institution, and in so doing you have made yourself irrelevant.”

A third Trump pick is also likely to not advance further, after retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) placed a hold on Michael LoSapio, nominated to be the new director for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

Tillis objected to LoSapio after the nominee said in his confirmation hearing that the Capitol was not attacked on Jan. 6, 2021.

articles.summary: One company has bid and provisionally won the rights to mine off the coast of American Samoa as the Trump administration pushes for offshore mining. Wetstone US Ventures provisionally acquired the two leases to mine off the coast, a spokesperson for the Marine Minerals Administration said. The company was the only bidder during an auction…
articles.body:
One company has bid and provisionally won the rights to mine off the coast of American Samoa as the Trump administration pushes for offshore mining.

Wetstone US Ventures provisionally acquired the two leases to mine off the coast, a spokesperson for the Marine Minerals Administration said. The company was the only bidder during an auction for the mining rights leases Thursday.

The area encompasses a combined 31.5 million acres of U.S. federal waters.

Large-scale deep-sea mining has never been done before, but it’s something the Trump administration has pushed for as another avenue for shoring up U.S. supply chains.

“American manufacturers rely on critical minerals to build advanced electronics, energy infrastructure and equipment for our national defense, but heavy reliance on overseas suppliers leaves manufacturers vulnerable when those supplies are disrupted. That’s why this sale is a critical first step in our offshore energy strategy,” acting Marine Minerals Administration Director Mike Olsen said ahead of the auction.

Environmental organizations have opposed such efforts, warning that they could be harmful to ocean ecosystems.

“This premature push to exploit the deep sea before we even fully understand how vital it is will have catastrophic consequences that reverberate for generations,” Oceana Defense Campaign Manager Julia Singer said in a written statement. “The Trump administration has clearly put corporate interests above the health and well-being of our oceans.”

Meanwhile, the leases also face a potential legal snafu. A federal judge ruled this week that the administration did not adequately consider the potential impacts to endangered species.

While her ruling did not explicitly block the lease sale from happening, Judge Jill Otake also said in a separate but related case that “any bidders for the leases will be on notice” that the administration violated the Endangered Species Act.

A spokesperson for the Marine Minerals Administration said via email that in order to address the issues raised by the court, the agency has “initiated formal incremental step consultation” with the National Marine Fisheries Service that covers more than the initial Endangered Species Act review.

articles.title: US Lawmakers Near Deal to Ban Chinese Cars in Lame Duck Session
articles.summary: Lawmakers in Washington are closing in on a deal to ban Chinese cars from the US, according to people familiar with the matter, following last-minute negotia...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Lawmakers in Washington are closing in on a deal to ban Chinese cars from the US, according to people familiar with the matter, following last-minute negotiations aimed in part at sparing Mercedes-Benz Group AG, which is nearly 20% owned by Chinese entities.

Republicans and Democrats from auto-producing states driving the effort aim to send a bill to President Donald Trump's desk by the end of the year, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the deliberations are private. If enacted, the profitable US car market would be walled off to automakers such as BYD Co. and Geely Automobile Holdings Inc., whose low-cost, technology-packed electric vehicles have rapidly gained market share in Europe and South America.

Details about the measure are still being hammered out. Republican Senator Bernie Moreno on Wednesday briefed automaker representatives on changes under consideration to earlier legislation that aimed to block Chinese connected vehicles from the US, including provisions that would shield Mercedes from an outright ban, said the people.

Automaker representatives were broadly supportive of the effort Moreno described, though a Mercedes official voiced reservations and negotiations remain underway, the people said. Proponents are working to pass the measure before the next Congress begins in January, the people said.

"We continue to meet with all stakeholders who have a shared interest in ensuring this important legislation becomes law in this Congress," Mercedes said in a statement.

Chinese cars are effectively shut out of the US because of steep tariffs and restrictions on Chinese vehicle technology imposed by the Commerce Department. Enshrining a ban into law would take those measures a step further to address growing concerns about national and economic security threats posed by China's ambition to dominate the global auto industry.

A bill advanced by a Senate panel earlier this year would have prohibited manufacturers that are more than 15% owned by Chinese entities from selling cars equipped with technology that can transmit data. Mercedes, which has lobbied for changes to that bill, is nearly 10% owned by China's BAIC Motor Corp., a state-owned carmaker.

The USS George Washington, a Japan-based aircraft carrier, departed the Middle East, leaving the U.S. military with two aircraft carriers in the U.S. Central Command (Centcom) region, a military official confirmed to The Hill’s sister network NewsNation.
